tasks.title: Agentic loops
tasks.body_html:
• Lifecycle: send request → check stop_reason → if "tool_use", execute tools and append results to history → loop. On "end_turn", stop.
  • Know the difference between model-driven decisions (the model picks the next tool) and pre-configured sequences (your code fixes the order).
Anti-patterns: parsing natural language ("I'm done") to detect completion · using an iteration cap as the main stop condition · treating any assistant text as the completion signal.

tasks.title: Coordinator–subagent orchestration
tasks.body_html:
• Hub-and-spoke: the coordinator owns all routing, error handling and communication. Subagents don't talk to each other.
  • Subagents have isolated context and don't inherit the coordinator's history.
  • The coordinator decomposes, delegates, aggregates, and chooses subagents based on how complex the query is.
  • Refine iteratively: check the synthesis for gaps → re-delegate → re-synthesize.
Narrow decomposition leaves gaps. If a report covers only part of a topic, blame the coordinator's assignments, not the subagents.

tasks.title: Subagent invocation & context passing
tasks.body_html:
• The coordinator's allowedTools must include "Task".
  • Define each subagent with an AgentDefinition: description, system prompt, tool restrictions.
  • Pass context explicitly in the prompt, with complete findings in a structured format that keeps content separate from metadata (URL, doc name, page).
  • Emit parallel Task calls in one coordinator response for independent work.
  • Fork sessions to explore different approaches.
  • Coordinator prompts should state goals and quality criteria, not rigid step-by-step procedures.

tasks.title: Multi-step workflows with enforcement
tasks.body_html:
• Programmatic gates (hooks, prerequisites) give deterministic compliance. Prompt guidance always has some failure rate.
  • Example: block process_refund (and lookup_order) until get_customer returns a verified ID.
  • Split multi-concern requests, investigate the parts in parallel, then synthesize.
  • Hand off to humans with a structured summary: customer ID, root cause, amounts, recommended action.
Financial, identity or compliance requirement → code, not prompt.

tasks.title: Agent SDK hooks
tasks.body_html:
• PostToolUse: normalize mixed data (Unix timestamps, ISO 8601, numeric status codes) before the model sees it.
  • Interception (pre-tool) hooks: block policy violations, e.g. refunds over $500, and redirect them to human escalation.
  • When a rule must be guaranteed, use a hook instead of a prompt.

tasks.title: Task decomposition
tasks.body_html:
• Fixed prompt chaining fits predictable multi-aspect work. Dynamic decomposition fits open-ended investigation.
  • For large code reviews, do per-file passes plus a cross-file integration pass.
  • For open-ended work (e.g. adding tests to a legacy codebase): map the structure → find high-impact areas → build a prioritized plan that adapts as dependencies show up.

tasks.title: Session state
tasks.body_html:
• --resume <session-name> continues a named session.
  • fork_session branches from a shared baseline.
  • When resuming, tell the session which files changed so it re-analyzes only those.
  • If earlier tool results are stale, start fresh with an injected summary instead of resuming.

tasks.title: Tool interfaces
tasks.body_html:
• The tool description is the main signal the model uses to choose a tool.
  • Good descriptions include input formats, example queries, edge cases, and how the tool differs from similar tools.
  • Rename or split overlapping tools, e.g. split a generic analyze_document into purpose-specific tools.
  • Check the system prompt for keyword-heavy wording that overrides good descriptions.
The model picks the wrong tool and the descriptions are minimal → the first step is to expand the descriptions.

tasks.title: Structured MCP error responses
tasks.body_html:
• Set isError. Distinguish transient, validation, business, permission errors.
  • Return errorCategory, isRetryable, and a readable description.
  • Subagents retry transient failures locally and escalate only what they can't resolve, along with partial results and what they tried.
  • Keep access failures separate from valid empty results.
A generic "Operation failed" leaves the agent no way to recover.

tasks.title: Tool distribution & tool_choice
tasks.body_html:
• Too many tools (18 vs 4–5) makes selection worse. Scope tools to each agent's role, plus a few cross-role tools for frequent needs.
  • Swap generic tools for constrained ones: load_document instead of fetch_url.
  • tool_choice: "auto" (model decides) · "any" (must call some tool) · {"type":"tool","name":"…"} (forces that tool).

tasks.title: MCP integration
tasks.body_html:
• Project .mcp.json for shared team tools · user ~/.claude.json for personal or experimental servers.
  • Use env var expansion (${GITHUB_TOKEN}) so secrets aren't committed.
  • Tools from all connected servers are available at once.
  • Write detailed MCP tool descriptions so the agent doesn't fall back to built-ins like Grep.
  • Use community servers for standard integrations (Jira). Build custom ones only for team-specific needs.
  • Expose content catalogs as MCP resources to cut down on exploratory calls.

tasks.title: Built-in tools
tasks.body_html:
• Grep searches file contents · Glob matches file-name patterns · Read/Write handle whole files · Edit makes targeted changes using a unique anchor.
  • If Edit fails on a non-unique match → fall back to Read + Write.
  • Build understanding step by step: Grep for entry points → Read to follow imports → trace exported names across modules.

tasks.title: CLAUDE.md hierarchy
tasks.body_html:
• Levels: user ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (not shared) · project .claude/CLAUDE.md or root · directory level.
  • @import for modular files. .claude/rules/ for topic files (e.g. testing.md).
  • /memory shows which files are loaded, which is how you debug "why is it ignoring X?"

tasks.title: Commands and skills
tasks.body_html:
• .claude/commands/ holds shared project commands. ~/.claude/commands/ holds personal ones.
  • Skills: .claude/skills/ SKILL.md with frontmatter: context: fork (runs as an isolated sub-agent), allowed-tools (restricts tools), argument-hint (prompts for parameters).
  • Make personal variants under a different name so teammates aren't affected.
  • Skills load on demand. CLAUDE.md is always loaded.
Command definitions don't go in CLAUDE.md, and there is no config.json "commands" array.

tasks.title: Path-specific rules
tasks.body_html:
• .claude/rules/*.md with YAML paths: globs (e.g. terraform/**/*) load only when matching files are edited.
  • Globs like **/*.test.tsx apply a convention across directories. Subdirectory CLAUDE.md files can't do this cleanly.

tasks.title: Plan mode vs direct execution
tasks.body_html:
• Plan mode: large, multi-file, architectural work with several valid approaches (microservice split, 45+ file migration).
  • Direct execution: clear, well-scoped changes (single-file fix).
  • Use the Explore subagent to keep verbose discovery out of the main context. Common pattern: plan, then execute.

tasks.title: Iterative refinement
tasks.body_html:
• When prose instructions get read inconsistently, give 2–3 concrete input/output examples.
  • Write tests first, then iterate on the failures.
  • Interview pattern: have Claude ask questions to surface considerations in unfamiliar domains before it implements.
  • Send interacting issues together in one message. Fix independent issues one at a time.

tasks.title: CI/CD integration
tasks.body_html:
• -p / --print for non-interactive runs (fixes a pipeline that hangs waiting for input).
  • --output-format json + --json-schema → machine-parseable findings that can become PR comments.
  • On re-review: include earlier findings and report only new or unaddressed issues.
  • Give it the existing tests so it doesn't generate duplicates. Document testing standards and fixtures in CLAUDE.md.
  • Run reviews in a session independent of the one that wrote the code.

tasks.title: Explicit criteria
tasks.body_html:
• Specific categorical criteria ("flag comments only when they contradict the code") work better than vague ones like "be conservative."
  • Say what to report (bugs, security) and what to skip (minor style).
  • Temporarily turn off categories with high false-positive rates to rebuild developer trust.
  • Define severity levels with concrete code examples.

tasks.title: Few-shot prompting
tasks.body_html:
• Use 2–4 targeted examples for ambiguous cases, and show the reasoning behind each chosen action.
  • Show the output format (location, issue, severity, fix).
  • Contrast acceptable patterns with real issues to cut false positives.
  • Cover varied document structures to reduce empty or hallucinated extractions.

tasks.title: Structured output via tool use
tasks.body_html:
• Tool use with a JSON schema guarantees syntax, not semantics (line items can still fail to sum to the total).
  • tool_choice: "any" when the document type is unknown · forced tool to guarantee a specific extraction runs first.
  • Make fields nullable/optional when the source may lack them, so the model doesn't invent values.
  • Enums should include "unclear" and "other" plus a detail field. Pair strict schemas with format normalization rules.

tasks.title: Validation & retry loops
tasks.body_html:
• On retry, send the original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation errors.
  • Retries fix format and structure errors. They can't fix information that isn't in the source (e.g. it's in an external document you didn't provide).
  • Add detected_pattern fields to track false-positive patterns.
  • Self-checking fields: calculated_total vs stated_total, conflict_detected.

tasks.title: Batch processing
tasks.body_html:
• Message Batches API: 50% cheaper, results within 24 h, no latency SLA, no multi-turn tool calling.
  • Use it for latency-tolerant work (overnight reports, weekly audits), not for blocking checks (pre-merge).
  • Match requests to responses with custom_id. Resubmit only the failed items, and split any that exceeded limits.
  • Tune the prompt on a sample before a large run.
  • Plan the cadence against the SLA: submission window + 24 h ≤ SLA (4-hour windows meet a 30-hour SLA).

tasks.title: Multi-instance & multi-pass review
tasks.body_html:
• A model is less likely to question its own reasoning within the same session, so review with an independent instance.
  • Do per-file passes plus a cross-file integration pass.
  • Have the model report confidence per finding so you can route reviews.

tasks.title: Preserving context
tasks.body_html:
• Progressive summarization flattens numbers, dates and promises made to the customer. Keep a persistent "case facts" block outside the summarized history.
  • In multi-issue sessions, keep each issue's data separate.
  • Trim verbose tool output (40+ fields when 5 matter).
  • "Lost in the middle": put key findings at the start and use clear section headers.
  • Subagents return structured data with metadata, not long reasoning. Always pass the complete history in later requests.

tasks.title: Escalation & ambiguity
tasks.body_html:
• Escalate when: the customer explicitly asks for a human (do it right away) · there's a policy gap or exception · no meaningful progress is possible.
  • Frustrated customer with a simple issue: acknowledge, offer a resolution, and escalate only if they ask again.
  • Policy is silent (competitor price match when policy covers only your own site) → escalate.
  • Multiple matching records → ask for more identifiers, don't guess.
Sentiment and self-reported confidence are unreliable signals of complexity.

tasks.title: Error propagation in multi-agent systems
tasks.body_html:
• Return structured context: failure type, attempted query, partial results, alternatives.
  • Keep timeouts separate from valid empty results.
  • Synthesis output should note coverage gaps.
Anti-patterns: returning empty results as success on failure · killing the whole workflow because one part failed · generic status messages.

tasks.title: Large codebase exploration
tasks.body_html:
• Long sessions degrade, and the model starts falling back on "typical patterns."
  • Keep a scratchpad file of key findings · hand verbose investigation to subagents · summarize each phase before starting the next.
  • Crash recovery: each agent exports its state to a known location, and a manifest is loaded on resume.
  • Run /compact when discovery output fills the context.

tasks.title: Human review & confidence calibration
tasks.body_html:
• An aggregate accuracy figure (97%) can hide weak performance on particular document types or fields. Break accuracy down by type and field before cutting review.
  • Use stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions to measure errors and catch new patterns.
  • Have the model output field-level confidence and calibrate thresholds against a labeled validation set.
  • Send low-confidence or contradictory items to humans, prioritizing where reviewers' limited time goes.

tasks.title: Provenance & uncertainty in synthesis
tasks.body_html:
• Compressing findings without claim→source mappings loses attribution. Require structured mappings (source, document, excerpt).
  • When statistics conflict, report both with attribution rather than picking one.
  • Require publication or collection dates, since a difference over time isn't a contradiction.
  • Separate established findings from contested ones. Format by content type: tables for financials, prose for news, lists for technical findings.

rules.trigger: A requirement with financial, identity or compliance stakes is sometimes skipped
rules.action: Programmatic prerequisite or hook. Prompts are probabilistic.

rules.trigger: The model picks the wrong tool and the descriptions are thin
rules.action: Expand the descriptions first (formats, examples, edge cases, boundaries)

rules.trigger: An agent has 15+ tools and selection is poor
rules.action: Scope 4–5 tools per role, plus a few shared tools for frequent needs

rules.trigger: Loop stops early or runs forever
rules.action: Drive it with stop_reason (tool_use → continue, end_turn → stop)

rules.trigger: Subagent output ignores earlier findings
rules.action: Subagents don't inherit history, so pass context explicitly in the prompt

rules.trigger: The coordinator can't spawn subagents
rules.action: Add "Task" to allowedTools

rules.trigger: Independent subagent jobs run one after another
rules.action: Emit parallel Task calls in one coordinator response

rules.trigger: A research report misses whole subtopics
rules.action: The coordinator's decomposition was too narrow

rules.trigger: Mixed formats from tools confuse the model
rules.action: PostToolUse hook to normalize

rules.trigger: A subagent times out or fails
rules.action: Structured error: type, query, partial results, alternatives. Don't hide it or abort everything.

rules.trigger: Agent can't tell 'no results' from 'couldn't reach the source'
rules.action: Return access failures and valid empty results differently

rules.trigger: Team needs a shared slash command
rules.action: Put it in .claude/commands/ in the repo

rules.trigger: Conventions for files scattered across the repo
rules.action: Use .claude/rules/ with a paths: glob

rules.trigger: Personal preference that shouldn't affect the team
rules.action: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md or a personal skill under a different name

rules.trigger: Large or architectural change with several valid approaches
rules.action: Plan mode first

rules.trigger: Clear single-file fix
rules.action: Direct execution

rules.trigger: CI job hangs waiting for input
rules.action: claude -p / --print

rules.trigger: Need PR comments from the review
rules.action: --output-format json + --json-schema

rules.trigger: Large PR gets inconsistent review results
rules.action: Per-file passes + a cross-file integration pass

rules.trigger: Self-review misses its own mistakes
rules.action: Use an independent instance or session to review

rules.trigger: Too many false positives from a reviewer
rules.action: Explicit categorical criteria plus few-shot contrasts. Temporarily turn off noisy categories.

rules.trigger: Extraction invents values for missing fields
rules.action: Make the fields nullable or optional

rules.trigger: Values don't fit the enum
rules.action: Add "other" + a detail field, and "unclear"

rules.trigger: The JSON is valid but the numbers don't add up
rules.action: Schemas only guarantee syntax, so add calculated vs stated fields and a conflict flag

rules.trigger: Retrying won't fix the extraction
rules.action: The info isn't in the source. Retries only fix format and structure.

rules.trigger: Latency-tolerant bulk job
rules.action: Batch API. Never use it for blocking or pre-merge checks or multi-turn tool use.

rules.trigger: Unknown document type with several extraction tools
rules.action: tool_choice: "any"

rules.trigger: A particular extraction must run first
rules.action: Force it with tool_choice {type:"tool", name}

rules.trigger: Customer explicitly asks for a human
rules.action: Escalate immediately

rules.trigger: Policy doesn't cover the request
rules.action: Escalate

rules.trigger: Several customer records match
rules.action: Ask for more identifiers

rules.trigger: Someone proposes routing on sentiment or self-confidence
rules.action: Wrong answer. Use explicit criteria with examples, or calibrated, validated confidence.

rules.trigger: Summaries lose amounts and dates
rules.action: Keep a persistent case-facts block outside the summary

rules.trigger: 97% overall accuracy, should we cut human review?
rules.action: Break it down by doc type and field first, and use stratified sampling

rules.trigger: Sources give conflicting statistics
rules.action: Report both with attribution and dates

rules.trigger: Long exploration session starts drifting
rules.action: Scratchpad file, subagents, phase summaries, /compact

flashcards.back_html: "tool_use": run the requested tools, append the results to history, and send again. "end_turn" means stop. Trap: a reply can contain text and a tool request. If you stop because there's text, the tool call never runs.

Parsing natural language to detect completion · an iteration cap as the main stop condition · treating assistant text as the completion signal. Why: all three guess from the wording or a counter. stop_reason is the structured signal. Keep a cap only as a backstop.

flashcards.front: Do subagents see the coordinator's conversation?
flashcards.back_html: No. They have isolated context, so pass everything they need explicitly in the Task prompt. Exam tell: "the subagent's output is generic / ignores the findings" means the context was never passed in its prompt.

flashcards.front: What must the coordinator's allowedTools include?
flashcards.back_html: "Task", which is needed to spawn subagents. Exam tell: the coordinator plans delegation but every subagent call is "not permitted". Check allowedTools before anything else.

A description, a system prompt, and tool restrictions for the subagent. Why: the description tells the coordinator when to delegate, and tool restrictions keep the subagent least-privileged. Task context goes in the prompt, not the definition.

flashcards.front: How do you run subagents in parallel?
flashcards.back_html: Emit several Task tool calls in a single coordinator response. Trap: only independent work goes in parallel. A step that needs earlier results (synthesis) waits for them.

flashcards.front: Hook vs prompt: when do you need the hook?
flashcards.back_html: Whenever the rule must be guaranteed (financial limits, identity checks, compliance). Prompts have a nonzero failure rate. Trap: capital letters, repetition and extra few-shot examples are all still prompts. If the stem says compliance, money or fraud, the answer is a hook or gate.

Normalizing mixed tool output (Unix vs ISO timestamps, numeric status codes) before the model sees it. Why: the model never has to convert formats, so it can't get the conversion wrong. You also don't need to change the MCP server.

Fixed chaining for predictable multi-aspect tasks. Dynamic decomposition for open-ended investigation that adapts as you learn. Exam tell: "same three checks on every PR" points to fixed chaining. "Legacy codebase, unknown dependencies" points to dynamic decomposition.

--resume <name> continues a named session. fork_session branches into separate approaches from a shared baseline. Trap: subagents don't inherit history and /compact keeps a summary, so neither gives you isolated branches. Use fork_session for that.

flashcards.front: Resumed session but the files changed: what do you do?
flashcards.back_html: Tell it which files changed so it re-analyzes only those. If the old tool results are broadly stale, start fresh with an injected summary. Rule of thumb: a few files changed → resume and name them. Most of it changed (big refactor) → start fresh with a summary.
Customer ID, root cause, amounts, and the recommended action. Why: the human shouldn't have to re-read a 30-message transcript. Raw logs, sentiment scores and full reasoning are distractors.

flashcards.front: Main signal the model uses to select a tool
flashcards.back_html: The tool description: input formats, example queries, edge cases, and how it differs from similar tools. Exam tell: two tools with near-identical one-line descriptions. The first fix is better descriptions, not a router or a merge.

Transient, validation, business, permission. Return them with isError, errorCategory, isRetryable and a readable message. Why: the category and isRetryable tell the agent whether to retry, fix its input, or stop and explain. "Operation failed" tells it nothing.
"auto" (model decides) · "any" (must call some tool) · {"type":"tool","name":"x"} (must call x). Trap: "any" forces some tool, not a particular one. To guarantee a specific first call, name the tool.
Few, around 4–5 scoped to the role. 18 tools makes selection worse. Why: accuracy drops as near-miss options pile up. When descriptions are already detailed, split into role-scoped agents.

Project-scoped and shared (committed) vs user-scoped for personal or experimental servers. Trap: CLAUDE.md doesn't configure MCP servers. An experimental personal server belongs in ~/.claude.json, not the shared file.

flashcards.front: How do you keep secrets out of .mcp.json?
flashcards.back_html: Environment variable expansion, e.g. ${GITHUB_TOKEN}. Trap: committing a token to a "private" repo still breaks policy. It stays in git history.

flashcards.front: Agent ignores your MCP search tool and uses Grep
flashcards.back_html: Improve the MCP tool's description so the model knows when to prefer it. Trap: disabling Grep or renaming the tool "grep2" is heavy-handed. Say when your tool beats Grep, and when Grep is still the better choice.

Community for standard integrations (Jira, GitHub). Custom only for team-specific needs. Why: don't spend your time rebuilding a mature integration. Save custom work for internal systems that have no public server.

flashcards.front: Why expose a catalog as MCP resources?
flashcards.back_html: It gives the agent a map of the content, so it makes fewer exploratory tool calls. Why: the agent sees what exists up front instead of spending 10–15 list/search calls finding out.
Grep searches file contents. Glob matches file names/paths. Exam tell: "files matching a pattern, then where X is called" means Glob first, then Grep.

flashcards.front: Edit fails on a non-unique match
flashcards.back_html: Use a longer unique anchor, or fall back to Read + Write. Trap: don't delete "duplicate" lines to make the anchor unique. They're working code.

User ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (not shared) · project .claude/CLAUDE.md or root · directory level. Exam tell: "only for me, every repo" means the user level. "Teammate doesn't get it" usually means it was put at the user level by mistake.

flashcards.front: How do you see which CLAUDE.md files are loaded?
flashcards.back_html: Run /memory. Why: it's the fastest diagnosis for "Claude ignores my instructions". Check what's loaded before rewriting anything.

flashcards.front: Make a rule load only for Terraform files
flashcards.back_html: .claude/rules/terraform.md with frontmatter paths: ["terraform/**/*"]. Why: specialized conventions in the root CLAUDE.md load into every session and dilute the rest. Path-scoped rules load only when relevant.
.claude/commands/ (repo, shared) vs ~/.claude/commands/ (personal). Trap: no "commands" array exists in .claude/config.json. Commands are Markdown files in .claude/commands/.

context: fork (isolated sub-agent), allowed-tools (restrict tools), argument-hint (prompt for parameters). Exam tell: "verbose output crowds the context" → context: fork. "Must not write files" → allowed-tools.
Skills load on demand. CLAUDE.md is always loaded. Why: a long checklist needed a few times a month belongs in a skill. In CLAUDE.md it costs tokens in every session.
Large, multi-file or architectural changes with several valid approaches. Exam tell: a clear stack trace pointing to one line → direct execution. 60 files with several viable designs → plan mode.

Have Claude ask you questions to surface considerations before it implements something in an unfamiliar domain. Why: it brings up requirements you didn't know to state (retention, tamper-evidence, and so on) before any code exists.

Send interacting issues together in one message. Fix independent ones one at a time. Trap: splitting a cause from its symptom risks a patch for the symptom only. Mixing in an unrelated typo makes review harder.
-p / --print. Exam tell: a CI job "hangs until timeout" → add -p. For a script to parse results, add --output-format json with --json-schema.
Include the earlier findings and report only new or unaddressed issues. Why: re-posting fixed issues trains developers to ignore the bot. Each run should add new signal.

flashcards.front: Why is 'be conservative' a bad instruction?
flashcards.back_html: It's vague. Use explicit categorical criteria for what to report and what to skip. Trap: "very conservative" or "only important issues" is still vague. Say which categories to report and which to skip.

flashcards.front: How many few-shot examples, and what should they show?
flashcards.back_html: 2–4 targeted examples of ambiguous cases, with the reasoning behind each decision. Trap: 20 random examples are mostly easy cases. One long "perfect review" doesn't show where the line is.

flashcards.front: What does a JSON schema via tool use guarantee?
flashcards.back_html: Syntax and structure, not semantic correctness. Why: a schema-valid output can still have line items that don't add up. You still need semantic checks in code.
Make fields nullable or optional when the source may not have them. Why: a required field pushes the model to invent a plausible value. A regex won't catch a well-formed fake.

Include "unclear" and "other" plus a free-text detail field. Why: without a way out, statements and credit memos get forced into the nearest category. The detail field also tells analytics what's arriving.

flashcards.front: What goes into a retry prompt?
flashcards.back_html: The original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation errors. Trap: sending only the error message. The model can't fix an extraction it can't see, from a document it doesn't have.
When the information isn't in the source at all. Exam tell: "the clause is in a document you didn't provide" means a retry can't help. Route it to a human or get the source.
50% cheaper · up to 24 h · no latency SLA · no multi-turn tool calling. Rule: anything blocking or interactive (pre-merge checks, live chat) or anything needing tool loops stays off the Batch API.

flashcards.front: How do you match batch results to requests?
flashcards.back_html: custom_id. Resubmit only the failed ones. Why: you fix and resubmit only what failed, and change the oversized requests first, so they don't fail again.
calculated_total vs stated_total, conflict_detected, detected_pattern. Why: the model reports a contradiction instead of hiding it, and code can route it for review.

Transactional facts (amounts, dates, promises) kept outside the summarized history so they don't get flattened. Trap: summarizing more often compresses more and loses more. Exact figures need a block that never gets summarized.
Put key findings at the start and use clear section headers. Trap: repeating the input twice doubles the cost and pushes even more material into the middle.

Explicit request for a human · policy gap or exception · no meaningful progress possible. Trap: "explain the policy first, then escalate if they ask again". An explicit request for a human is honored right away.
Customer sentiment and the model's self-reported confidence. Why: sentiment doesn't track complexity (calm customers have hard disputes), and self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated.
Ask for more identifiers. Never guess. Trap: showing all three accounts to the customer leaks other people's data. Ask for an email, order number or ZIP code.

flashcards.front: What a failed subagent should return
flashcards.back_html: Failure type, attempted query, partial results, alternatives. Why: the coordinator can retry, rephrase or report the gap. An empty "success" makes the report claim nothing exists.

Scratchpad files, subagent delegation, phase summaries, /compact, and manifests for crash recovery. Why: tool output that piles up is what makes long sessions go generic. Keep findings somewhere durable and keep verbose work out of the main context.

flashcards.front: Before reducing human review at 97% accuracy
flashcards.back_html: Stratify by doc type and field, sample high-confidence items, calibrate against labeled data. Trap: "97% overall" can hide a weak field (say, total_amount) or one vendor's layout. Measure it broken down by type and field.
Report both with source attribution and dates, and separate established from contested findings. Trap: picking one figure or averaging them. Different dates may just be a trend, not a conflict.

Model-driven: the model picks the next tool. Pre-configured: your code fixes the order. When the order must be guaranteed, use code. Exam tell: "leadership wants the order guaranteed for audit" means it's enforced in code. A weekly log of deviations isn't prevention.

flashcards.front: A rule with financial, identity or compliance stakes
flashcards.back_html: Enforce it in code with a prerequisite or hook, not in the prompt. Prompts always have some failure rate. Why: a 2% failure rate on fraud or compliance is still a breach. Gates make the rule hold whatever the conversation looks like.

Split the concerns, investigate them in parallel with separate data, then reply with one combined answer. Trap: escalating just because a message has two issues, or answering one and asking the customer to open a new chat for the other.

flashcards.front: Report misses whole subtopics, every subagent did its job
flashcards.back_html: The coordinator's decomposition was too narrow. Fix the assignments. Why: when each subagent did its task well and coverage is still missing, the fault is the plan, not the workers.

flashcards.front: Refinement loop for a research synthesis
flashcards.back_html: Check the synthesis for gaps → re-delegate the missing parts → re-synthesize. Trap: having synthesis fill the gaps from general knowledge produces uncited claims in a cited report.

Through the coordinator (hub-and-spoke). Subagents never talk to each other directly. Why: routing, observability and error handling all stay in one place. Peer-to-peer calls hide work from the coordinator.

flashcards.front: Passing findings to a synthesis subagent
flashcards.back_html: Explicitly, in the prompt, as structured findings that keep content separate from metadata (URL, document, page). Why: citations can't come loose from their claims. A one-line summary or the raw concatenated pages both lose attribution.

flashcards.front: An interception hook blocks a refund. Then what?
flashcards.back_html: Redirect to human escalation with the case details. Never hide the block or allow a workaround. Trap: splitting $900 into two $450 refunds, or capping it at $500 automatically. Both work around the control.
Per-file passes plus a cross-file integration pass. Trap: 40 independent reviews with no combined step also miss cross-file breaks, such as a changed signature and its callers.
Start a fresh session with an injected summary instead of resuming. Trap: resuming or forking carries the stale context along. Start fresh and keep only the conclusions that still hold.

flashcards.front: What a good tool description includes
flashcards.back_html: Input formats, example queries, edge cases, and how the tool differs from similar tools. Why: the model chooses tools mostly from their descriptions. "Searches data" on two tools makes it a coin toss.

flashcards.front: Good descriptions, wrong tool still chosen
flashcards.back_html: Check the system prompt for keyword-heavy wording that overrides the descriptions. Exam tell: descriptions are already good, but one tool gets called on "hi". Look for SHOUTED instructions in the system prompt.

flashcards.front: One generic tool doing several jobs
flashcards.back_html: Split or rename it into purpose-specific tools, e.g. analyze_document → extract_tables, check_compliance. Why: a tool that does several jobs pushes the real choice into free-text instructions. Separate tools each get the right parameters.

flashcards.front: Fields in a structured MCP error
flashcards.back_html: isError, errorCategory (transient · validation · business · permission), isRetryable, and a readable description. Exam tell: a business error isn't retryable (a refund outside the window). A transient one is (a timeout or 429).

flashcards.front: A subagent hits a transient failure
flashcards.back_html: Retry locally. Escalate only what it can't resolve, with what it tried and any partial results. Why: a short blip is absorbed close to where it happened. A lasting failure reaches the coordinator with useful context, not "Operation failed".

Prefer constrained tools: load_document keeps an agent inside its role, while fetch_url opens up anything. Why: a description asking it to "stick to vetted sources" is a soft rule. A tool that can only load approved IDs enforces it.

Tools from all connected servers are available at once, so descriptions must be distinct. Why: you can combine tools in one task, such as reading a PR and updating its Jira ticket. Tools don't override each other.

Grep for entry points → Read to follow imports → trace exported names across modules. Trap: reading every file alphabetically, or adding logging to explore. Explore incrementally and follow real usage.
Use @import for modular files and .claude/rules/ for topic files (e.g. testing.md). Why: separate files per topic mean clearer owners, fewer merge conflicts, and path-scoped loading where it helps.

flashcards.front: Where command definitions do NOT go
flashcards.back_html: Not in CLAUDE.md, and there is no config.json "commands" array. Use .claude/commands/. Trap: ~/.claude.json isn't shared through the repo either. Only committed files under .claude/ reach the team.
Runs the skill as an isolated sub-agent, so its output stays out of the main conversation. Exam tell: "reads 200 log files and returns a one-paragraph answer" is a good fit for context: fork.
SKILL.md frontmatter that prompts for parameters when the skill runs. Exam tell: people keep running the skill without a required name, and Claude invents one.
SKILL.md frontmatter that restricts the tools the skill can use, e.g. read-only. Exam tell: "it bumped versions in package.json during an audit". Limit it to read-only tools.
Keeps verbose discovery out of the main context. Common pattern: explore, plan, then execute. Why: planning needs room for the earlier constraints. Discovery that fills the context pushes them out.
Write tests first, then iterate on the failures. Why: tests check every edge case on every iteration, so fixes stop breaking other cases.
Give it the existing tests, and document testing standards and fixtures in CLAUDE.md. Trap: batching, more iterations and JSON output don't change what Claude knows about your fixtures.
Define each severity level with concrete code examples. Trap: "high = serious, medium = moderate" defines words with other vague words.

flashcards.front: A checkable criterion for outdated comments
flashcards.back_html: "Flag a comment only when it contradicts the code." Why: "might be outdated" can't be checked. "Contradicts the code" can be verified against the code.

flashcards.front: What few-shot examples should show about output
flashcards.back_html: The format: location, issue, severity, fix. Why: the model copies the structure it sees, so few-shot examples fix inconsistent shapes even before you add a schema.
Few-shot examples that cover varied document structures. Trap: making every field required fills empty extractions with invented line items.

Pair the schema with format normalization rules (e.g. ISO 8601 dates). Why: the dates are already found correctly. Only the format needs pinning down, including how to handle ambiguous dates like 03/04/24.

When the source contradicts itself (two totals, two dates). Flag it for review instead of picking one. Trap: "take the later date" or "take the first clause". Silently picking a value has legal consequences.

flashcards.front: What the Batch API can't do
flashcards.back_html: Multi-turn tool calling within a request, and anything that needs a latency SLA. Exam tell: an extraction calls a lookup tool and then continues. Restructure it (look up beforehand) or keep it synchronous.
Tune the prompt on a sample first. Why: problems found after 100,000 documents are expensive to redo. A few hundred representative documents expose them cheaply.

Submission window + 24 h ≤ SLA. Example: 4-hour windows meet a 30-hour SLA. Worked example: 8-hour windows give 8 + 24 = 32 h (missed). 4-hour windows give 4 + 24 = 28 h (met). The longest allowed window is SLA − 24 h.

flashcards.front: Two issues in one support chat
flashcards.back_html: Keep each issue's data in its own block so details don't cross over. Exam tell: "applied order A's refund to order B". Merging or summarizing the cases makes it worse.
Trim the output to what matters before it enters the context. Trap: "tell the model to ignore the extra fields". Ignored fields still take up context. Trim them in a PostToolUse hook.
Escalate. Don't guess at records or loop forever. Trap: picking the closest-matching order on an unverified account, or closing the chat with "try again later".
Say so: the synthesis should note its coverage gaps. Why: readers know which section rests on thinner evidence. Filling gaps from general knowledge adds uncited claims.
Use field-level confidence and calibrate against a labeled validation set. Trap: a flat 0.9 for every field. Raw scores can be overconfident, and fields differ in difficulty.

Tables for financials, prose for news, lists for technical findings. Separate established findings from contested ones. Why: each audience finds its material in a form it can scan, such as comparable numbers in a table.

questions.prompt: Your customer support agent is built on the Agent SDK with the tools get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund and escalate_to_human. The loop exits when Claude's reply contains "Let me know if you need anything else." In production, about 4% of refund conversations end with the customer told "your refund is on its way" while process_refund was never called. Transcripts show Claude wrote the closing phrase in the same response where it requested a tool call. What is the most reliable fix?
questions.explanation: The API already tells you whether the model wants to keep working: stop_reason is "tool_use" when it has requested a tool and "end_turn" when it is finished. Parsing natural language for completion is a guess, and it fails when text and a tool call arrive together.

choices.text: Raise the max iteration count from 5 to 15 so the agent has more turns to finish the refund
choices.why: The loop isn't running out of turns. It exits early on a phrase, so more iterations never get used.

choices.text: Drive the loop with stop_reason: continue on "tool_use", exit on "end_turn"
choices.why: Correct. This is the structured signal for loop control, and it handles responses that contain both text and a tool request.

choices.text: Add a system prompt rule that the closing phrase may only be used after every requested task is complete
choices.why: This lowers the failure rate but doesn't remove it. The exit decision still rests on the model's wording.

choices.text: Replace the exact phrase match with a regex that recognises several common closing phrases
choices.why: This catches more phrasings but has the same flaw: text in the reply says nothing about whether a tool call is pending.

questions.prompt: While reviewing the support agent's design, an engineer proposes ending the agentic loop after exactly 8 iterations, because "in our tests, every conversation finished within 8 turns, and a fixed count makes cost predictable." Most conversations finish in 3 to 5 turns, but complex multi-order refunds have needed up to 11 in staging. What is the best response?
questions.explanation: stop_reason is the primary stop condition. An iteration cap is still useful, but only as a safety net against runaway loops, and it should sit well above the longest legitimate run.

choices.text: Agree, since a fixed iteration count is the recommended way to bound both cost and latency in agentic loops
choices.why: A fixed count cuts off legitimate long conversations (the 11-turn refunds) and keeps nothing else in check.

choices.text: Stop on stop_reason, and keep a cap only as a guard against runaway loops
choices.why: Correct. The loop ends when the model is done, and a generous cap still bounds a pathological case.

choices.text: Raise the fixed count to 12 so it covers the longest case seen in staging, and keep it as the stop condition
choices.why: It no longer cuts off the known cases, but simple conversations would keep looping after the model is done, and the next longer case breaks it again.

choices.text: Ask the model to include a JSON flag such as {"done": true} in its text, and stop the loop when it appears
choices.why: This rebuilds a weaker version of stop_reason out of free text the model may forget or mis-format.

questions.prompt: Your multi-agent research system has a coordinator that runs web-search and document-analysis subagents. Their findings come back to the coordinator as tool results. The coordinator then spawns a synthesis subagent with the prompt "Write the final report on the topic using the research findings." The report is fluent but generic. It cites none of the sources the search subagent found and contradicts two of the analysis subagent's conclusions. What is the root cause?
questions.explanation: Subagents start with a fresh context. They do not see the coordinator's conversation, so anything they need, here the findings and their sources, has to be in the prompt the coordinator writes for them.

choices.text: The synthesis subagent uses a smaller model than the coordinator and can't handle long reports
choices.why: Model size wouldn't explain why it ignores every finding. It never received them.

choices.text: Subagents don't inherit the coordinator's history, so the findings were never in its prompt
choices.why: Correct. The prompt refers to "the research findings" but doesn't contain them, so the subagent wrote from general knowledge.

choices.text: The coordinator's allowedTools is missing "Task", so the synthesis subagent ran without its tools
choices.why: If "Task" were missing the subagent couldn't be spawned at all. It did run.

choices.text: The synthesis subagent should have been started with fork_session so it could read the parent conversation
choices.why: Forking is for branching a session to explore alternatives. Passing context explicitly in the prompt is the intended pattern for subagents.

questions.prompt: You are building the research system's coordinator with the Agent SDK. You defined four subagents with AgentDefinition, each with a description, system prompt and tool list. When you run a query, the coordinator writes a sensible plan ("I'll delegate the literature search to the search agent…"), but no subagent ever runs. The logs show the coordinator's attempts to invoke a subagent are rejected as not permitted. What should you check first?
questions.explanation: Subagents are invoked through the Task tool. If the coordinator's allowedTools doesn't include "Task", every delegation attempt is refused, however well the subagents are defined.

choices.text: Whether each AgentDefinition has a detailed system prompt describing its role and output format
choices.why: A thin system prompt hurts output quality, but it doesn't make invocation rejected.

choices.text: Whether "Task" is in the coordinator's allowedTools
choices.why: Correct. "Not permitted" points to a permissions problem, and Task is the tool that spawns subagents.

choices.text: Whether every subagent has been given access to the same MCP servers that the coordinator itself uses
choices.why: Subagent tool access affects what they can do once running. It doesn't stop the coordinator from spawning them.

choices.text: Whether tool_choice is set to "any" so the coordinator is forced to call a tool on every turn
choices.why: Forcing a tool call doesn't grant permission. A forbidden tool would still be rejected.

questions.prompt: For a broad query, the research coordinator splits the work into four independent subtopics and delegates each to a search subagent. Each subagent takes about 40 seconds. The trace shows the coordinator emits one Task call, waits for the result, emits the next, and so on, so the research phase takes almost three minutes. The subtopics don't depend on each other. What is the best fix?
questions.explanation: Independent subagents can run in parallel when the coordinator emits several Task calls in a single response. Sequential calls are only needed when one result feeds the next.

choices.text: Merge the four subagents into one search subagent that has all the tools and covers all four subtopics
choices.why: One agent working through four subtopics is still sequential, and you lose the focus and isolated context of separate subagents.

choices.text: Have the coordinator emit all four Task calls in one response
choices.why: Correct. The calls run in parallel, and the research phase drops to roughly the time of the slowest subagent.

choices.text: Move the four subtopic searches to the Message Batches API so they are processed concurrently
choices.why: Batches can take up to 24 hours and don't support the multi-turn tool use a search subagent needs.

choices.text: Lower each subagent's max_tokens so that every one of them finishes in less time
choices.why: This trims a little time per call and risks truncated findings. The calls are still serial.

questions.prompt: Company policy says any refund over $500 must be approved by a human. The support agent's system prompt states this in a dedicated section, with two few-shot examples of escalating a large refund. A monthly audit finds that 3% of refunds over $500 were still processed automatically, usually in long conversations where the customer was persistent. Finance says any automatic large refund is a compliance breach. What should you implement?
questions.explanation: When a rule must hold every time and a violation is costly, enforce it in code. Prompt instructions and examples lower the failure rate but never make it zero.

choices.text: Restate the $500 rule in capital letters at both the start and the end of the system prompt
choices.why: Stronger wording is still probabilistic. Long, persistent conversations are exactly where emphasis wears off.

choices.text: Add more few-shot examples that show the agent refusing large refunds from persistent customers
choices.why: More examples may lower the 3%, but compliance needs zero, and examples can't promise that.

choices.text: A hook on process_refund that blocks amounts over $500 and routes them to escalate_to_human
choices.why: Correct. The check runs outside the model on every call, so the policy holds whatever the conversation looks like.

choices.text: Ask the model to state its confidence before each refund, and block the refund whenever confidence is low
choices.why: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated, and the failing refunds may well come with high confidence.

questions.prompt: The support agent uses three MCP tools from different teams. get_customer returns dates as Unix epochs, lookup_order returns ISO 8601 strings, and the billing tool returns "MM/DD/YY". When customers ask whether an order arrived within the 30-day return window, the agent sometimes compares dates across formats and gets it wrong. You can't change the MCP servers this quarter. What is the most reliable place to fix this?
questions.explanation: PostToolUse hooks run in code after a tool returns and before the model sees the result. They are the place to normalize heterogeneous tool output deterministically.

choices.text: A PostToolUse hook that normalizes every date to ISO 8601 before the model sees it
choices.why: Correct. Every result arrives in one format, so the model never has to convert, and the fix needs no server changes.

choices.text: A system prompt section that explains each tool's date format and tells the agent to convert before comparing
choices.why: The model has to do the conversion correctly every time, which is the error you are trying to remove.

choices.text: A separate date-conversion subagent that the support agent can call whenever it needs to compare two dates
choices.why: This adds latency and still relies on the agent deciding to call it.

choices.text: Few-shot examples of correct cross-format date comparisons, including epochs and two-digit years
choices.why: This improves the odds but leaves the arithmetic with the model. A deterministic transform is more reliable.

questions.prompt: Your team asks you to use Claude to add meaningful test coverage to a 200k-line legacy service. It has no tests, little documentation, and dependencies between modules that nobody fully understands. Some modules turn out to be dead code, and others are called from everywhere. You want the effort spent where it reduces the most risk. Which approach fits best?
questions.explanation: Open-ended work with unknown structure calls for dynamic decomposition: explore first, then build a plan that adapts as you learn. Fixed prompt chains suit work whose steps are known in advance.

choices.text: A fixed prompt chain that generates tests for each file in alphabetical order, one file per step
choices.why: This spends equal effort on dead code and critical hubs, and can't adapt when dependencies turn up.

choices.text: Map the structure, find high-impact areas, and follow a prioritized plan that adapts
choices.why: Correct. Exploring first shows where the risk is, and an adaptive plan copes with what you discover along the way.

choices.text: One prompt asking Claude to add tests everywhere they are needed across the service in a single pass
choices.why: A single pass over 200k lines loses detail and gives you no way to prioritize.

choices.text: Send every source file through the Message Batches API overnight with a generate-tests prompt
choices.why: Cheap, but each file is handled in isolation, with no view of dependencies or priority.

questions.prompt: Yesterday you spent two hours in a named Claude Code session analysing a payments service: 40 files, a dependency map, and a list of risky code paths. This morning you see that a teammate merged a change touching 3 of those 40 files. The rest of the analysis still applies. You want to continue with as little rework as possible. What should you do?
questions.explanation: Resuming keeps the earlier context. When only a few inputs changed, tell the session exactly which files changed so it re-reads those instead of trusting stale tool results.

choices.text: Resume the session and say which 3 files changed so it re-analyzes just those
choices.why: Correct. You keep the two hours of context and refresh only what went stale.

choices.text: Start a brand-new session and re-run the whole 40-file analysis from scratch to be safe
choices.why: Safe but wasteful. 37 of the 40 files haven't changed.

choices.text: Resume the session without mentioning the change, since Claude will notice modified files on its own
choices.why: The session's earlier tool results show the old contents. Claude has no reason to re-read files it thinks it already knows.

choices.text: Fork the session from yesterday's state and delete the original once the fork is running
choices.why: Forking is for branching into alternatives. It doesn't refresh the stale files.

questions.prompt: You and Claude Code have finished a shared analysis of a legacy billing module: its call graph, its invariants and its test gaps. Now you want to try two competing refactoring strategies (extracting a service vs. restructuring in place), each building on that analysis. You don't want the exploration of one strategy to bias or clutter the other, and you want to compare the results afterwards. What should you use?
questions.explanation: fork_session branches a session from a shared baseline. Each branch keeps the common context and diverges independently, which suits exploring alternatives.

choices.text: Use --resume twice with the same session name, once for each refactoring strategy in turn
choices.why: Both runs would continue the same session, so the second strategy would see the first.

choices.text: fork_session from the shared baseline, one branch per strategy
choices.why: Correct. Both branches start from the same analysis and stay isolated from each other.

choices.text: Spawn two subagents that inherit the main session's history, one exploring each strategy
choices.why: Subagents don't inherit history, so they would start without the analysis.

choices.text: Run /compact on the session between the two attempts so the first strategy is summarised away
choices.why: Compaction still carries a summary of the first attempt, so the second isn't independent of it.

questions.prompt: When the support agent escalates to a human, it calls escalate_to_human with the conversation transcript. Human agents complain that they spend the first 5 minutes of every handoff re-reading 30-message transcripts to find out who the customer is, what went wrong and what they are supposed to do. Handoff resolution time is twice the target. What should the escalate_to_human payload contain? (Select TWO.)
questions.explanation: A handoff should stand on its own: who the customer is, what is at stake, what the agent found, and what it recommends. The human shouldn't have to reconstruct the case.

choices.text: The customer ID and the amounts involved
choices.why: Correct. The human can pull up the account and see the stakes immediately.

choices.text: The root cause found and a recommended action
choices.why: Correct. The human starts from the agent's diagnosis instead of redoing it.

choices.text: The model's full reasoning for every turn of the conversation, so the human can follow its logic
choices.why: This is even longer than the transcript the humans already find too long.

choices.text: A sentiment score for each customer message, plotted across the conversation
choices.why: Possibly interesting, but it doesn't say who the customer is or what to do.

choices.text: A link to the raw tool-call logs, with the transcript removed to keep the payload small
choices.why: This replaces one thing to dig through with another.

questions.prompt: The research coordinator's system prompt is a 14-step numbered procedure: "1. Search for definitions. 2. Search for history. 3. Search for current statistics…" and so on. For standard topics it works. For comparative questions ("How do EU and US approaches differ?") or narrow technical ones, it still runs all 14 steps, wastes calls on irrelevant searches, and misses angles the steps never anticipated. What is the recommended change?
questions.explanation: Coordinators work best when the prompt states goals and quality criteria and leaves the decomposition to the model. Rigid procedures break on inputs they didn't anticipate.

choices.text: Add more numbered steps to cover comparative and narrow technical questions as special cases
choices.why: Each new query type needs more steps, and the procedure still breaks on the next shape you didn't foresee.

choices.text: State goals and quality criteria, and let the coordinator decide how to decompose
choices.why: Correct. The coordinator adapts the plan to the question while the criteria keep quality consistent.

choices.text: Replace the coordinator with a fixed pipeline of subagents, one for each of the 14 steps
choices.why: This hard-codes the same rigid procedure in architecture instead of in a prompt.

choices.text: Set tool_choice so the coordinator is forced to delegate to a subagent at every one of the steps
choices.why: This forces more calls, including the irrelevant ones that are already the problem.

questions.prompt: The support agent has two MCP tools: search_orders, described as "Searches data", and search_customers, also described as "Searches data". Both take a single query string. Logs show that about 1 in 6 calls goes to the wrong tool. Customer emails get passed to search_orders, and order numbers to search_customers, so the agent then tells customers it can't find them. What is the best first step?
questions.explanation: The model chooses tools mostly from their descriptions. When two descriptions are vague and identical, start by fixing them. That's the cheapest change and it goes straight at the root cause.

choices.text: Merge them into one search tool with a type parameter that says which kind of record to search
choices.why: This might help eventually, but the model still has to pick the type, and it has no better guidance for that.

choices.text: Build a keyword-based router in front of the model that sends each query to a tool by its pattern
choices.why: This adds infrastructure to cover for a documentation gap, and it breaks on queries that don't fit the patterns.

choices.text: Rewrite both descriptions with input formats, example queries and when to use the other tool
choices.why: Correct. The model can now tell an order number from an email address and knows which tool fits each.

choices.text: Add 20 few-shot examples of correct tool choices to the system prompt
choices.why: This helps a little, but it costs tokens on every request and leaves the root cause, the vague descriptions, in place.

questions.prompt: An internal MCP server wraps your inventory system. It returns {"content": "Operation failed"} for every failure: timeouts, malformed SKUs and permission denials alike. Agents using it retry everything, so a permission denial gets retried until the loop's cap is hit, and malformed SKUs are re-sent unchanged. Your on-call team is tired of the noise. What is the best fix?
questions.explanation: Structured errors let the agent react correctly: retry transient failures, fix validation errors, and stop on business or permission errors. A generic error string leaves the agent guessing.

choices.text: Tell the agents in their system prompts never to retry after any error from the inventory server
choices.why: Timeouts would then fail even though a retry would have worked.

choices.text: Return isError with an errorCategory, an isRetryable flag and a readable description
choices.why: Correct. Each kind of failure now tells the agent what to do next.

choices.text: Return the HTTP status code as plain text in the content field instead of the generic failure message
choices.why: This is a bit more informative, but the agent has to interpret raw codes and still gets no clear retry signal.

choices.text: Log every error on the server side and return an empty successful result to the agent
choices.why: This hides failures as successes, which is worse than the generic message.

questions.prompt: Your research system started as one generalist agent with 18 tools: web search, PDF parsing, citation formatting, translation, charting and more. As tools were added, quality dropped. The agent often picks a near-miss tool, for example parse_html for a PDF or format_citation_apa when MLA was asked for. The descriptions are already detailed. What is the recommended architecture change?
questions.explanation: Tool-selection accuracy drops as the number of tools grows. Scoping agents to a role with roughly 4–5 tools each, plus a few shared tools for frequent needs, keeps every choice manageable.

choices.text: Make all 18 descriptions longer still, and keep the single generalist agent
choices.why: The descriptions are already detailed. The problem is the number of overlapping options.

choices.text: Split it into role-scoped agents with about 4–5 tools each, plus a few shared tools
choices.why: Correct. Each agent chooses from a short, relevant list, and the coordinator routes the work.

choices.text: Set tool_choice to "any" so that the generalist agent always calls one of its tools
choices.why: Forcing a call doesn't help the agent choose the right one.

choices.text: Switch to a larger model, which can keep all 18 tools and their descriptions in mind at once
choices.why: This may help at the margins, but costs more and doesn't fix the design problem.

questions.prompt: Your structured-extraction pipeline processes contracts, invoices and letters. Downstream systems need extract_metadata (document type, parties, dates) to run first, before any other extraction tool, on every document. Some documents begin with text like "Summarize the payment terms below," and the model then calls extract_payment_terms first. How do you guarantee extract_metadata runs first?
questions.explanation: tool_choice set to a specific tool forces that tool on the request. It's the deterministic way to make a particular call happen first, whatever the input says.

choices.text: Set tool_choice to "auto" and add a system prompt instruction to always call extract_metadata first
choices.why: This is probabilistic, and the documents' own instructions are already pulling the model away from it.

choices.text: Set tool_choice to "any" so that the model must call one of its tools on the first request
choices.why: This forces some tool call, but not necessarily extract_metadata.

choices.text: Set tool_choice to {"type":"tool","name":"extract_metadata"} on the first request
choices.why: Correct. The first call is guaranteed, and later requests can go back to "auto".

choices.text: Put extract_metadata first in the tools array, since the model favours the earliest tool listed
choices.why: Tool order isn't a control mechanism, and it guarantees nothing.

questions.prompt: Your team of eight uses Claude Code with a GitHub MCP server. Right now each person has configured it by hand, and settings have drifted. You want one shared configuration in the repo so new hires get it automatically. Security policy forbids committing tokens, and each developer uses a personal access token. What should you do?
questions.explanation: Project-scoped servers go in .mcp.json, committed at the repo root. Secrets are referenced with environment-variable expansion, so each developer supplies their own token.

choices.text: Put the server in each developer's ~/.claude.json with their token written directly into the file
choices.why: This is user scope. Nothing is shared, so the drift continues.

choices.text: Commit .mcp.json at the project root, with the token referenced as ${GITHUB_TOKEN}
choices.why: Correct. Everyone shares one configuration, and no secret is committed.

choices.text: Commit .mcp.json with a shared token in it, and rely on the repository being private
choices.why: This breaks the security policy. Private repos still leak, and the token ends up in git history.

choices.text: Describe the server configuration in CLAUDE.md so Claude Code can set it up for each developer
choices.why: CLAUDE.md holds instructions. Claude Code doesn't load MCP servers from it.

questions.prompt: Your platform team built an MCP server exposing code_search, which queries a semantic index over 30 repositories and answers conceptual questions ("where do we validate refunds?") far better than text matching. Its description reads "Searches code." It's configured correctly and works when called by name, but transcripts show agents use the built-in Grep for over 90% of searches, including conceptual ones. What is the most likely fix?
questions.explanation: When a capable custom tool is ignored in favour of a built-in, the cause is usually a thin description. Say what the tool is good at, give example queries, and say when the built-in is still the better choice.

choices.text: Disable Grep for the whole organization so agents have to use code_search for every search
choices.why: Grep is still the right tool for exact-string lookups, so this breaks good behaviour to force adoption.

choices.text: Describe when code_search beats Grep, such as conceptual queries across repos
choices.why: Correct. The model now knows when to choose it, and it still uses Grep where Grep fits.

choices.text: Rename the MCP tool to "grep2" so that agents see it as a direct replacement for the built-in Grep
choices.why: Agents might call it for exact matches, where it's worse, and they still wouldn't understand what it's for.

choices.text: Move the MCP server from project scope to user scope so its tools are loaded earlier in each session
choices.why: Scope controls who gets the server, not how the model chooses between tools.

questions.prompt: Your team wants Claude Code to work with Jira (read tickets, update status, add comments) and with your company's internal deployment-approval system, which has a custom REST API and its own permission model. A well-maintained community Jira MCP server exists. There's no public server for the approval system. You have two weeks. What is the best approach?
questions.explanation: Use a mature community MCP server for a standard integration, and build custom servers only for systems that are unique to your organization.

choices.text: Build custom MCP servers for both Jira and the approval system, so the team controls every part of both
choices.why: Rebuilding Jira support duplicates existing work and eats into the two weeks.

choices.text: Use the community Jira server, and build a custom server only for the approval system
choices.why: Correct. Your effort goes where nothing already exists.

choices.text: Use Bash with curl commands for both systems instead of setting up any MCP servers
choices.why: Raw curl gives you no structured tools, no error handling and no clear tool descriptions.

choices.text: Adapt a community server written for some other approval tool, and use it for the internal system as well
choices.why: A server built for another system won't match your internal API or permission model.

questions.prompt: In the research system, a subagent's lookup_publication tool queries an internal citations database. It returns [] when nothing matches, but also returns [] when the database is unreachable. During last week's database outage, several reports confidently stated that "no prior publications exist" on topics that have dozens. Why is this a problem, and what is the fix?
questions.explanation: An empty result and an access failure mean very different things. Return a structured error when the source couldn't be reached, and keep [] for a genuine "none found".

choices.text: It isn't a real problem, because an empty list correctly says no results were returned
choices.why: The outage reports show it is a problem. An outage was treated as a finding.

choices.text: An outage looks like "none found". Return a structured error for failures, keep [] for no matches
choices.why: Correct. The agent can then retry, report the gap, or tell the reader that coverage is limited.

choices.text: Return null in both cases instead of [], so the agent treats every result with more caution
choices.why: The two cases still look the same, just with a different value.

choices.text: Have the tool retry every empty result three times before returning it to the agent
choices.why: This adds latency to every real empty result and still returns [] if the outage lasts.

questions.prompt: You are using the Agent SDK's built-in tools to audit a large TypeScript monorepo. First you need a list of every test file matching src/**/*.spec.ts. Then you need to find which of those files call createUser(, so you can check how test users are set up. Which built-in tools fit, and in what order?
questions.explanation: Glob matches file names and paths. Grep searches file contents. Find the set of files first, then search inside them.

choices.text: Grep, then Glob
choices.why: Grep searches contents and Glob matches paths, so this runs them in the wrong order for the task.

choices.text: Glob, then Grep
choices.why: Correct. Glob finds the spec files, and Grep finds the createUser( calls inside them.

choices.text: Read, then Edit
choices.why: Neither tool finds files. Edit changes files, and this is a read-only audit.

choices.text: Bash ls, then Read every file
choices.why: This works but is slow and wasteful. You'd read thousands of lines to find one pattern.

questions.prompt: An agent is fixing a bug in a 900-line service file. Its Edit call fails with an error saying the old_string "return null;" isn't unique, because it appears 6 times in the file. The agent knows which occurrence it wants: the one inside validateSession(). The fix is a one-line change. What should the agent do next? (Select TWO.)
questions.explanation: Edit needs a unique anchor. Either widen the anchor with surrounding context until it is unique, or fall back to reading the file and writing the full updated version.

choices.text: Retry Edit with a longer anchor that is unique, including the surrounding lines
choices.why: Correct. Adding lines from inside validateSession() makes the match unique.

choices.text: Fall back to Read the file, then Write the full updated version
choices.why: Correct. It's heavier, but it works when no short unique anchor exists.

choices.text: Use Glob to look for a different file that contains the same validation logic
choices.why: The bug is in this file. Looking elsewhere doesn't fix it.

choices.text: Delete the five duplicate lines first so that "return null;" only appears once
choices.why: This deletes working code just to satisfy the tool, and would break the other functions.

choices.text: Switch tool_choice to "any" and try the same Edit call again
choices.why: tool_choice has no effect on how Edit matches text.

questions.prompt: You built a documentation assistant on MCP. Before answering, agents make 10 to 15 exploratory list_docs and search_docs calls just to find out what documentation exists: which products, which versions, which sections. Latency and cost are high, and the answers are fine once the agent finds the right page. What MCP feature cuts down this exploration?
questions.explanation: MCP resources expose read-only content such as catalogs and schemas up front, so the agent can see what exists without spending tool calls to discover it.

choices.text: Exposing the documentation catalog as MCP resources
choices.why: Correct. The catalog is available as context, so the exploratory calls go away.

choices.text: Adding a short sleep between tool calls so the agent paces its exploration
choices.why: This makes latency worse and doesn't reduce the number of calls.

choices.text: Adding more fine-grained list tools so each exploratory call returns less data
choices.why: More tools means more calls and more choices to get wrong.

choices.text: Moving the exploratory calls to the Message Batches API to make them cheaper
choices.why: Batches are asynchronous and don't fit interactive multi-turn tool use.

questions.prompt: A developer on your team likes very terse, single-line commit messages and wants Claude Code to write them that way in every repository they work in. The team's project CLAUDE.md asks for conventional commits with a body paragraph, and teammates rely on that format. The developer doesn't want to change anything for anyone else. Where does their instruction go?
questions.explanation: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md holds personal preferences that apply across all of one person's projects and aren't shared with anyone else.

choices.text: In the project-root CLAUDE.md, under a section for personal preferences
choices.why: The project CLAUDE.md is committed and shared, so every teammate would get the terse style.

choices.text: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md
choices.why: Correct. It's user-level, applies in every repo they work in, and affects no one else.

choices.text: In a .claude/rules/commits.md file in the repo, scoped to commit-related paths
choices.why: Rules files in the repo are shared with the team, and commits aren't a file path anyway.

choices.text: In a team slash command, /terse-commit, that they run whenever they want to commit
choices.why: A team command is shared, and they'd have to remember to run it every time.

questions.prompt: Your team's testing conventions (Vitest, factories instead of fixtures, no snapshot tests) are written in packages/web/CLAUDE.md. While working in packages/web/src, Claude keeps writing snapshot tests with fixtures, as if it has never seen the conventions. Before you rewrite anything, you want to know whether that CLAUDE.md is being loaded at all. What is the fastest way to check?
questions.explanation: /memory shows which memory files (CLAUDE.md and others) are loaded in the current session. It's the quickest way to diagnose "Claude is ignoring my instructions."

choices.text: Run /memory
choices.why: Correct. It lists the loaded memory files, so you can see right away whether packages/web/CLAUDE.md is among them.

choices.text: Restart Claude Code and check whether the conventions are followed in the new session
choices.why: This is slow and indirect. You'd be guessing from behaviour instead of checking what's loaded.

choices.text: Run /compact so the conversation is summarized and the instructions are reloaded
choices.why: Compaction summarizes the conversation. It doesn't tell you which files are loaded.

choices.text: Copy the conventions into a slash command and run it before each testing task
choices.why: This works around the problem without finding out what it is.

questions.prompt: Your monorepo has a terraform/ directory with 300 lines of conventions: module layout, naming, required tags and state-backend rules. They only matter when someone edits Terraform. Most sessions are frontend or API work, and putting the conventions in the root CLAUDE.md made those sessions noticeably worse at following the conventions that do apply to them. What is the best setup?
questions.explanation: Path-scoped rules in .claude/rules/ with paths frontmatter load only when Claude works on matching files. Specialized conventions stay out of unrelated sessions.

choices.text: Keep them in the root CLAUDE.md, but move them to the end of the file under a clear heading
choices.why: They would still load into every session, which is what caused the problem.

choices.text: Create .claude/rules/terraform.md with frontmatter paths: ["terraform/**/*"]
choices.why: Correct. The conventions load automatically when Terraform files are involved, and not otherwise.

choices.text: Make a /terraform slash command that people have to remember to run before editing infra code
choices.why: Relying on people to remember is fragile. The rule should load by itself.

choices.text: Put a CLAUDE.md in every Terraform subdirectory, each holding a copy of the full conventions
choices.why: This duplicates 300 lines across directories, and the copies will drift.

questions.prompt: Your React app has test files (*.test.tsx) spread across 30 feature directories under src/features/. They all follow the same conventions: Testing Library queries by role, MSW for network calls, no implementation-detail assertions. Claude gets these right in some directories and wrong in others. You want one source of truth that applies whenever Claude touches a test file. What works best?
questions.explanation: A .claude/rules/ file with a glob in paths applies to matching files wherever they live, which suits conventions tied to a file type rather than a directory.

choices.text: A CLAUDE.md in each of the 30 feature directories, each containing the same test conventions
choices.why: Thirty copies means thirty places to update, and they will drift.

choices.text: A .claude/rules/ file with paths: ["**/*.test.tsx"]
choices.why: Correct. There's one file, and it applies to every test file in any directory.

choices.text: A skill that developers invoke before writing tests, which loads the conventions on demand
choices.why: This only helps when someone remembers to invoke it.

choices.text: One sentence in the root CLAUDE.md asking Claude to infer the conventions from nearby test files
choices.why: Inference is what's already giving inconsistent results.

questions.prompt: Your team wrote a /security-review command: a prompt template that checks the current diff for injection, auth and secrets issues. You want every developer to have it automatically when they pull the repo, with changes to it reviewed like code. Right now one person has it in their personal setup, and others have copied it by hand. Where should it live?
questions.explanation: Project slash commands are Markdown files in the repo's .claude/commands/ directory. They're committed and shared, and everyone gets them on git pull.

choices.text: ~/.claude/commands/security-review.md on each developer's machine
choices.why: That's user scope. It isn't shared or versioned with the repo.

choices.text: A "commands" array in .claude/config.json, committed alongside the code
choices.why: Claude Code has no such configuration mechanism.

choices.text: In the project CLAUDE.md, under a heading named /security-review
choices.why: CLAUDE.md holds instructions. It doesn't define slash commands.

choices.text: The repo's .claude/commands/security-review.md
choices.why: Correct. It's committed, reviewed in PRs, and available to everyone after a pull.

questions.prompt: Your team has a dependency-audit skill. When it runs, it produces pages of verbose output (every package, version and advisory) that push the actual conversation out of the main context. It should also never modify files. Last week it "helpfully" bumped versions in package.json during an audit. Which SKILL.md frontmatter fits? (Select TWO.)
questions.explanation: context: fork runs the skill as an isolated sub-agent, so its verbose work stays out of the main context. allowed-tools limits what the skill can do.

choices.text: context: fork
choices.why: Correct. The audit runs in isolation, and only its result comes back to the main conversation.
