choices.text: allowed-tools limited to read-only tools (e.g. Read, Grep, Glob)
choices.why: Correct. Without Write or Edit, it can't change package.json.

choices.text: argument-hint: "--verbose"
choices.why: This only hints at arguments. It wouldn't reduce output, and it suggests more.

choices.text: Loading the skill from CLAUDE.md with @import
choices.why: This would load it into every session, and it limits nothing.
This scopes when something applies. It does nothing for context or permissions.

questions.prompt: The team's /deploy-check skill lives in the repo's .claude/skills/deploy-check/ and is used by twelve engineers before every release. You want to try a modified version that adds a database-migration check. You're not sure it works yet, and you don't want anyone else's releases affected while you experiment. What should you do?
questions.explanation: Experiment in your personal scope under a different name, so the shared skill stays untouched until your version is proven.

choices.text: Edit the team skill directly while you test, and revert it later if the change doesn't work out
choices.why: Anyone who pulls in the meantime gets your untested version.

choices.text: Create a personal skill under a new name, e.g. ~/.claude/skills/deploy-check-exp
choices.why: Correct. Only you have it, and the team's skill isn't affected.

choices.text: Put your modified steps in the project CLAUDE.md so they apply alongside the existing skill
choices.why: The project CLAUDE.md is shared, so this changes everyone's behaviour.

choices.text: Copy it into the repo's .claude/skills/ under the same name, with your changes added
choices.why: This collides with the team's skill in the shared location.

questions.prompt: A user reports a crash, and the stack trace points to one line: user.profile.avatarUrl in components/Header.tsx, where profile is null for newly created accounts. The fix is clearly a null check plus a fallback avatar, and you know exactly where it goes. You're about to ask Claude Code to fix it. Which mode fits?
questions.explanation: Direct execution fits well-scoped changes whose location and solution are clear. Plan mode is for changes that are ambiguous, span many files, or involve real design choices.

choices.text: Plan mode, so Claude explores the component architecture before touching the header
choices.why: That's overhead for a one-line fix with a known location.

choices.text: Direct execution
choices.why: Correct. The scope is clear and small, so the fix can be made right away.

choices.text: An Explore subagent across the whole repo to find every other place profile could be null
choices.why: This could be a useful follow-up audit, but it isn't how to make this fix.

choices.text: A batch job that checks every component for similar null-pointer patterns overnight
choices.why: This doesn't fit an interactive one-line fix.

questions.prompt: You need to migrate authentication from session cookies to OAuth2 with JWTs. The change touches about 60 files: middleware, API routes, tests and the frontend auth context. There are several viable designs, such as token refresh in middleware vs. on the client, and where to store tokens. Choosing badly would mean significant rework. What is the best way to start?
questions.explanation: Plan mode lets Claude explore the codebase and compare approaches before editing. It fits large, multi-file changes with real design choices.

choices.text: Direct execution, with a detailed instruction describing the design you currently prefer
choices.why: This commits to a design before anyone has looked at how the 60 files depend on each other.

choices.text: Plan mode, to explore the code and compare approaches before editing
choices.why: Correct. You review a plan grounded in the actual code before any file changes.

choices.text: Direct execution, fixing problems and design issues as they come up during the migration
choices.why: Discovering design problems halfway through 60 files means expensive rework.

choices.text: Split it into 60 separate single-file prompts so each change stays small and reviewable
choices.why: Each change would be made without seeing the rest, so the design ends up inconsistent.

questions.prompt: You ask Claude Code to write a parseFlexibleDate helper. Your prose spec says it should "accept common date formats, handle relative dates sensibly, and reject ambiguous inputs." Over three attempts, Claude treated "03/04/2025" as March, then April, then rejected it, and handled "next Friday" differently each time. What is the most effective refinement?
questions.explanation: Concrete input → output examples remove ambiguity that prose leaves open. They're the fastest way to get consistent behaviour on edge cases.

choices.text: Rewrite the spec as longer, more formal prose that defines "common", "sensibly" and "ambiguous"
choices.why: This helps somewhat, but prose definitions still leave room for interpretation.

choices.text: Provide 2–3 concrete input → output examples, including the tricky cases
choices.why: Correct. "03/04/2025 → reject" and "next Friday → 2025-06-13 given today" settle it.

choices.text: Tell Claude to be careful about ambiguous dates and to think through each case before writing code
choices.why: Being told to be careful doesn't say which interpretation you want.

choices.text: Switch to plan mode so Claude designs the parsing rules before writing any code
choices.why: The plan would rest on the same ambiguous spec.

questions.prompt: Your CI pipeline adds a step that runs claude "review this diff for security issues" on each pull request. Locally the command works, but in CI the job hangs until the 30-minute timeout and posts nothing. The logs show Claude Code started and then produced no output. What is the fix?
questions.explanation: In CI, Claude Code has to run non-interactively. The -p (--print) flag runs the prompt, prints the result and exits, without waiting for interactive input.

choices.text: Pipe the output of the yes command into claude so any prompts are answered automatically
choices.why: This is a hack that doesn't make Claude Code non-interactive.

choices.text: Use claude -p "review this diff for security issues"
choices.why: Correct. Print mode runs once and exits, which is what CI needs.

choices.text: Set the environment variable CLAUDE_CI=true so Claude Code detects that it is running in CI
choices.why: This isn't a real setting, and it wouldn't change interactive mode.

choices.text: Add the --batch flag so the review is submitted as a non-interactive batch job
choices.why: Claude Code has no such flag. Batching is a separate API feature.

questions.prompt: Your CI review step works in -p mode and produces readable prose. Now you want a script to turn each finding into an inline PR comment on the right file and line, with a severity label. The first version parsed the prose with regexes and broke whenever the wording changed. Which invocation fits?
questions.explanation: For machine consumption, ask for structured output: --output-format json with --json-schema gives the script findings in a predictable shape.

choices.text: claude -p with --output-format json and --json-schema describing the findings
choices.why: Correct. Each finding has file, line, severity and message fields the script can rely on.

choices.text: Run claude in interactive mode in CI and capture screenshots of the findings for the script
choices.why: Screenshots aren't machine-readable, and interactive mode hangs in CI.

choices.text: Keep claude -p with plain-text output, and make the regex parser more forgiving
choices.why: This is the brittle approach that already failed.

choices.text: Run the review inside the PR author's own coding session and have them paste the results
choices.why: That's manual, it isn't independent, and it doesn't automate anything.

questions.prompt: Your CI reviewer posts findings as PR comments. On the first run it posts 12 comments. The developer pushes fixes for 9 of them. On the next run the reviewer posts all 12 again, including the 9 that are fixed. Developers have started ignoring the bot because of the noise. What should change?
questions.explanation: Give the reviewer its earlier findings and ask it to report only new or still-unaddressed issues, so each run adds signal instead of repeating itself.

choices.text: Delete all the old bot comments before every run so that the PR only shows the latest findings
choices.why: This hides the history but still asks developers to re-check fixed issues.

choices.text: Put the earlier findings in the prompt, and ask for only new or still-unaddressed issues
choices.why: Correct. The 9 fixed issues drop out, and only real remaining problems are posted.

choices.text: Only review the first commit of each PR, since that's where most issues are introduced
choices.why: Later commits can introduce new issues, and they would go unreviewed.

choices.text: Lower the model temperature so the reviewer's output is more stable from run to run
choices.why: Stable output would repeat the same 12 comments. The reviewer doesn't know what was fixed.

questions.prompt: A developer uses one Claude Code session to implement a feature over two hours. At the end, in the same session, they ask Claude to "review the changes for bugs." It reports only two minor style nits. A teammate reviewing by hand finds an off-by-one error and a missing authorization check. What is the better approach?
questions.explanation: A model reviewing its own work in the same context shares the assumptions that produced it. An independent session or instance reviews with fresh eyes.

choices.text: Ask the same session to review more harshly and assume there are at least three serious bugs
choices.why: Telling it to expect bugs pushes it to invent findings, and the shared blind spots remain.

choices.text: Run the review in an independent session or instance
choices.why: Correct. A fresh context doesn't carry the author's assumptions.

choices.text: Have the same session review the changes twice in a row and merge both lists of findings
choices.why: Two passes in the same context tend to repeat the same blind spots.

choices.text: Add "you are an expert security reviewer" to the review prompt in the same session
choices.why: A role line doesn't remove the context the session built while writing the code.

questions.prompt: Your CI review bot's prompt says "Be conservative and only flag important issues." Developers still get 15 to 20 comments per PR, mostly about variable naming, import order and missing trailing commas, and they've started to skim past all of them, including the occasional real bug. The linter already enforces style. What is the best improvement?
questions.explanation: Vague words like "conservative" and "important" mean different things to different readers. Spell out which categories to report and which to skip, and define severity with concrete code examples.

choices.text: Strengthen the wording to "be very conservative and flag only the most important issues"
choices.why: It's still vague. "Very important" is no better defined than "important".

choices.text: List categories to report and to skip, and show each severity level with code examples
choices.why: Correct. "Report bugs and security issues; skip style (the linter covers it)" removes the guesswork.

choices.text: Raise the temperature so the model is less fixated on surface-level style issues
choices.why: Temperature adds randomness. It doesn't define what counts as important.

choices.text: Ask the model to rate each finding's importance from 1 to 10, and drop anything under 7
choices.why: Self-ratings rest on the same undefined idea of importance and are poorly calibrated.

questions.prompt: Your review bot reports five categories of finding. Four of them (bugs, security, missing tests, API misuse) are accurate about 90% of the time. The fifth, "outdated comment", is wrong about 60% of the time, and developers have started to dismiss every bot comment without reading it, including valid security findings. You need trust back quickly. What should you do first?
questions.explanation: One noisy category can wreck trust in the whole tool. Turn that category off while you refine its criteria, and keep the accurate categories running.

choices.text: Turn off the bot entirely until every category is accurate enough to win developers back
choices.why: This throws away four accurate categories, including security findings.

choices.text: Temporarily disable the outdated-comment category while you refine its criteria
choices.why: Correct. The noise stops at once, and the useful findings keep coming.

choices.text: Require three independent reviewer runs to agree before any finding is posted to the PR
choices.why: This triples the cost, and the runs may agree on the same bad criteria.

choices.text: Post outdated-comment findings only in a weekly digest instead of on each PR
choices.why: This moves the noise somewhere else without fixing its accuracy.

questions.prompt: Your review bot handles clear-cut cases well but is inconsistent on judgement calls: a broad except that logs and re-raises, a TODO linked to a ticket, a magic number that's a well-known HTTP status code. You want to add few-shot examples to the prompt to make these calls consistent. Which design is most effective?
questions.explanation: The best few-shot examples are a few targeted ones that sit on the decision boundary, show the reasoning for flagging or not, and use the exact output format.

choices.text: One long example of a complete, perfect review of a realistic pull request
choices.why: One example can't cover the range of judgement calls, and it's mostly easy cases.

choices.text: 2–4 ambiguous cases with the reasoning, in the exact output format
choices.why: Correct. They show where the line is and why, in the format you want back.

choices.text: 20 randomly chosen examples of past review comments from the team's merged PRs
choices.why: Random examples are mostly easy cases, cost many tokens, and add inconsistent styles.

choices.text: Examples of real bugs only, so that the model learns what is worth flagging
choices.why: Without examples of acceptable patterns, the model can't tell where not to flag.

questions.prompt: Your invoice-extraction pipeline uses a tool with a JSON schema in which po_number is a required string. About 15% of invoices from small vendors have no purchase-order number. For those, the model returns plausible-looking values such as "PO-2024-0012", which the ERP then fails to match, causing payment delays. What schema change helps most?
questions.explanation: When a field can legitimately be missing, make it nullable or optional and say that null is correct when the value is absent. A required field pushes the model to invent one.

choices.text: Keep po_number a required string, and add a description saying not to invent values
choices.why: The schema still demands a string, so the model is still pushed to make one up.

choices.text: Make po_number nullable or optional, and say that null is correct when it's absent
choices.why: Correct. The model has a legitimate way to report "not present".

choices.text: Add a regex pattern to po_number so that only well-formed PO numbers are accepted
choices.why: Invented values like "PO-2024-0012" are well-formed and would pass.

choices.text: Raise max_tokens so the model has room to search the whole invoice for the PO number
choices.why: The PO number isn't there to find, and more tokens can't create it.

questions.prompt: Your extraction schema has a document_type enum of ["invoice", "receipt", "contract"]. The intake queue also receives account statements, credit memos and the occasional mis-scanned page. All of these come back as "invoice", get routed to accounts payable, and are rejected there by hand. Analytics also wants to know which other document types arrive, and how often. What is the best schema fix?
questions.explanation: Enums need a way out: "other" plus a detail field for types you didn't list, and "unclear" for documents that are genuinely ambiguous. Otherwise the model is forced into a wrong category.

choices.text: Add every document type you can think of to the enum, so that nothing is left uncategorized
choices.why: This never covers everything, and a long enum is harder to choose from accurately.

choices.text: Add "other" with a document_type_detail field, plus "unclear" for ambiguous documents
choices.why: Correct. Nothing is forced into "invoice", and the detail field shows analytics what's arriving.

choices.text: Remove the enum and use a free-text document_type field that the model fills in itself
choices.why: You lose consistent categories, and routing breaks on spelling variations.

choices.text: Make document_type a required field so the model always has to commit to a single category
choices.why: It's already effectively required. That's why everything is forced into "invoice".

questions.prompt: Every extraction from your invoice pipeline passes JSON schema validation. Even so, accounts payable reports that about 2% of invoices have line items that don't add up to the stated total. Sometimes the model misread a quantity, and sometimes the vendor's invoice is itself wrong. These go unnoticed until reconciliation, weeks later. What does this show, and how should you respond?
questions.explanation: A schema guarantees structure, not whether the values are right. Add semantic checks in code: extract both the calculated and the stated total, flag any mismatch, and route it for review.

choices.text: The JSON schema is defective, so switch to XML output, which can express stricter structure
choices.why: The structure is fine. The problem is the values, which no output format checks.

choices.text: Schemas check structure, not meaning: compare calculated and stated totals in code
choices.why: Correct. Mismatches are caught right away, whether the error is the model's or the vendor's.

choices.text: Use a forced tool_choice so the model always calls the extraction tool for every invoice
choices.why: The model already calls the tool. Forcing it changes nothing about the arithmetic.

choices.text: Raise the temperature so that the model explores more possible readings of each line item
choices.why: More randomness makes misread quantities more likely.

questions.prompt: You are adding a validation-and-retry loop to a contract-extraction pipeline. When validation fails, the pipeline retries with the document, the failed extraction and the error message. Your manager asks which failures you expect the loop to fix, and which should go straight to a human. Which validation failure is LEAST likely to be fixed by a retry with the error appended?
questions.explanation: Retries fix problems the model can correct from what it has: formats, types, details it overlooked. They can't fix information that isn't in the input.

choices.text: Dates returned as "March 3" instead of ISO 8601, which fails the date-format check
choices.why: This is a format error that a retry with the error message fixes easily.

choices.text: A missing required field whose value is actually on page 2 of the document provided
choices.why: The information is there. The error points the model to look again.

choices.text: A governing-law clause that exists only in a master agreement you didn't provide
choices.why: Correct. The information isn't in the input, so no retry can produce it.

choices.text: Amounts returned as strings like "1,200.00" instead of the numbers the schema expects
choices.why: This is a type error, and a retry with the error message usually fixes it.

questions.prompt: Your platform team is working out which Claude workloads to move to the Message Batches API to cut costs by 50%. Batches can take up to 24 hours to complete and don't support multi-turn tool calling within a request. The candidate workloads are listed below. Which workloads suit the Message Batches API? (Select TWO.)
questions.explanation: Batches suit high-volume work that isn't time-sensitive and needs one request per item. Avoid them for anything blocking, interactive or dependent on multi-turn tool use.

choices.text: A nightly technical-debt report across all repositories
choices.why: Correct. Nobody is waiting on it, and each repo is an independent request.

choices.text: A pre-merge security check that blocks every pull request until it passes
choices.why: A blocking check can't wait up to 24 hours.

choices.text: A weekly compliance audit of 50,000 archived documents
choices.why: Correct. It's high-volume, not urgent, and one request per document.

choices.text: An agent that needs several rounds of tool calls to process each item
choices.why: Batches don't support multi-turn tool calling within a request.

choices.text: Live chat support for customers on the website
choices.why: This is interactive. Customers can't wait hours for a reply.

questions.prompt: Your document pipeline must deliver extraction results within 30 hours of a document arriving. To save cost, you'll process documents with the Message Batches API, which can take up to 24 hours to complete a batch. Documents arrive steadily throughout the day, and each one waits for the next scheduled submission. What submission cadence meets the SLA in the worst case?
questions.explanation: Worst case = the longest wait for the next submission + the longest batch time. With a 24-hour batch window, the wait can be at most 6 hours, so submitting every 4 hours is the only option that meets 30 hours.

choices.text: Submit once a day
choices.why: Worst case is 24h waiting + 24h processing = 48h, which misses the SLA.

choices.text: Submit every 12 hours
choices.why: Worst case is 12h + 24h = 36h, which misses the SLA.

choices.text: Submit every 8 hours
choices.why: Worst case is 8h + 24h = 32h, which still misses the SLA by 2 hours.

choices.text: Submit every 4 hours
choices.why: Correct. Worst case is 4h + 24h = 28h, within the 30-hour SLA.

questions.prompt: A nightly 10,000-document extraction batch finishes with 140 failed requests. Looking at the errors, 128 failed for transient reasons and 12 failed because the request exceeded the size limit (very long scanned contracts). Results must be complete by morning, and you want to keep cost down. What is the right recovery?
questions.explanation: Recover selectively: use custom_id to identify the failures, resubmit only those, and change the requests that failed for structural reasons, here by splitting oversized documents.

choices.text: Resubmit all 10,000 documents as a new batch to make sure everything is consistent
choices.why: This repeats 9,860 successful requests and doubles the cost.

choices.text: Resubmit only the failures by custom_id, splitting the 12 oversized documents
choices.why: Correct. The transient failures get retried, and the oversized ones are fixed before resubmitting.

choices.text: Drop the 140 failures, since a 98.6% success rate is acceptable for a nightly batch
choices.why: Results have to be complete, so silently losing documents isn't acceptable.

choices.text: Resubmit all 140 unchanged, including the oversized ones, as synchronous real-time requests
choices.why: The 12 oversized requests will fail again whichever API you send them to.

questions.prompt: Your intake endpoint receives mixed uploads (invoices, W-9 tax forms and receipts), and each type has its own extraction tool. With tool_choice "auto", the model sometimes answers in prose ("This appears to be a W-9 form for…") instead of calling any tool, and the pipeline breaks. You don't know the document type in advance. Which tool_choice fits?
questions.explanation: "any" requires the model to call one of the tools but lets it choose which one. That suits cases where some extraction must happen and the right tool depends on the input.

choices.text: "auto"
choices.why: This is the current setting, and it allows the prose replies that break the pipeline.

choices.text: "any"
choices.why: Correct. A tool call is guaranteed, and the model picks the extractor that matches the document.

choices.text: Force extract_invoice for every upload
choices.why: W-9s and receipts would be pushed through the invoice extractor.

choices.text: No tools, and ask for JSON in the text response
choices.why: You lose schema-guided structure, and malformed JSON becomes possible.

questions.prompt: You are building the retry step of an extraction validation loop. When an extraction fails validation (for example, invoice_date isn't ISO 8601, or total is a string), the pipeline makes one more model call to fix it. A junior engineer's first version sends only "Validation failed: invoice_date must be YYYY-MM-DD" as the retry prompt. What should the retry prompt include?
questions.explanation: An effective retry gives the model everything it needs to correct itself: the source document, its previous output and the specific validation errors.

choices.text: Only the validation error message, which keeps the retry request small and focused
choices.why: The model can't fix an extraction it can't see, from a document it doesn't have.

choices.text: The original document, the failed extraction and the specific validation errors
choices.why: Correct. The model can see what it produced, what's wrong, and where to find the right value.

choices.text: The original document with an added instruction to try harder and be more accurate this time
choices.why: Without the specific errors, the model doesn't know what to fix.

choices.text: A different model's extraction of the same document, for the model to compare against
choices.why: This adds cost and confusion. The validation errors already say what's wrong.

questions.prompt: Your review bot posts 20 to 40 findings on large PRs. Reviewers want the riskiest findings at the top of the queue. The platform team wants to track which kinds of false positive keep coming back, so they can fix the prompt for those patterns. You're adding fields to the structured output schema. Which output fields help? (Select TWO.)
questions.explanation: Structured fields serve downstream needs. A confidence value lets you route or sort findings, and a pattern tag lets you analyse which kinds of finding are often wrong.

choices.text: A per-finding confidence value that is used for routing
choices.why: Correct. High-confidence or high-risk findings can be sorted to the top.

choices.text: A detected_pattern field tagging the type of finding
choices.why: Correct. You can count false positives by pattern and target the fixes.

choices.text: The model's favourite programming language, for context on how it reviews
choices.why: This is irrelevant to routing and to analysis.

choices.text: A field that repeats the full diff alongside each finding
choices.why: This bloats the output, and the diff is already available.

choices.text: A sentiment score for the code comments in the changed files
choices.why: This helps neither with prioritizing nor with analysing false positives.

questions.prompt: Your support agent summarizes older messages once a conversation passes 20 turns, to save context. QA finds that in long chats the summary turns "we'll refund $247.18 to your Visa ending 4421 by March 14" into "customer discussed a refund." Later in the chat, the agent can't confirm the amount or the date, and customers think it's backing out of the promise. What is the best fix?
questions.explanation: Summaries lose exact values. Keep critical facts (amounts, dates, IDs, commitments) in a persistent structured block outside the summarized history, so they survive compaction word for word.

choices.text: Stop summarizing, and send the full raw conversation history on every turn of long chats
choices.why: This avoids the loss but eventually runs out of context and drives up cost.

choices.text: Keep a "case facts" block of amounts, dates and commitments outside the summary
choices.why: Correct. The exact figures are kept word for word however much the conversation is compressed.

choices.text: Summarize more often, in smaller chunks, so that less detail is lost in each round
choices.why: More rounds of summarizing compound the loss of detail.

choices.text: Ask the customer to repeat the refund details whenever the agent needs to confirm them
choices.why: This annoys a customer who has already been given a commitment, and it hurts trust.

questions.prompt: The research coordinator passes the synthesis subagent about 60,000 tokens of findings from five subagents, concatenated in the order they arrived. Reviewers notice that findings in the middle of that input (usually from the third and fourth subagents) are often missing from the final report, even when they're among the most important. What helps? (Select TWO.)
questions.explanation: Models attend less reliably to material in the middle of long inputs. Put the most important content first, and give the input a clear structure with section headers.

choices.text: Put the key findings at the start of the input
choices.why: Correct. The most important material is in the position the model attends to best.

choices.text: Organize the input with clear section headers
choices.why: Correct. Structure makes every section easier to find and refer to.

choices.text: Repeat the full 60,000-token input twice so that every finding appears in two places
choices.why: This doubles the cost and pushes even more material into the middle.

choices.text: Render the findings in a smaller font so more of them fit in the context window
choices.why: Fonts mean nothing to a model. Tokens are what count.

choices.text: Remove all source metadata from the findings to shorten the input
choices.why: This shortens the input but loses the attribution the report needs.

questions.prompt: A customer's tracking shows "delivered" three days ago with a photo of a doorstep. The customer says the package never arrived, and that the doorstep in the photo isn't theirs. Their next message is: "I don't want to go through this with a bot. Can I please talk to a real person?" The agent could start a standard lost-package claim itself. What should the agent do?
questions.explanation: An explicit request for a human is an escalation trigger. Honor it right away, rather than first trying to resolve the issue or talk the customer out of it.

choices.text: Explain the tracking data and photo first, and escalate only if the customer asks again
choices.why: The customer has already asked clearly. Making them ask twice damages trust.

choices.text: Escalate to a human immediately
choices.why: Correct. Hand over with the tracking details and the photo discrepancy, so the human can act at once.

choices.text: Start the lost-package claim right away, which resolves the issue faster than a human would
choices.why: It may be efficient, but it ignores what the customer explicitly asked for.

choices.text: Ask the customer to rate how frustrated they are from 1 to 10 before deciding whether to escalate
choices.why: This adds friction and isn't a valid basis for the decision.

questions.prompt: A customer writes, irritated: "This is ridiculous. I ordered two weeks ago and it STILL hasn't shipped!" lookup_order shows the item is backordered, with a confirmed ship date in 4 days. The policy offers the option to cancel or switch to an in-stock alternative. The customer hasn't asked for a human, and nothing here falls outside policy. What is best?
questions.explanation: Frustration on its own isn't an escalation trigger. Acknowledge it, resolve what you can (date and options), and escalate if the customer then asks for a human.

choices.text: Escalate right away, because the customer is clearly frustrated and needs a human touch
choices.why: Sentiment isn't a reliable trigger, and this case is fully resolvable within policy.

choices.text: Acknowledge the frustration, give the date and options, and escalate if they then ask
choices.why: Correct. The customer gets an answer now, and a human is still available if they want one.

choices.text: Skip the acknowledgement and just give the ship date, since the facts are what matter
choices.why: It's accurate, but it ignores the frustration and makes the reply feel dismissive.

choices.text: Offer a 15% discount before anything else to defuse the frustration, then give the ship date
choices.why: This invents a remedy the policy doesn't include, and the real answer gets buried.

questions.prompt: A customer writes: "I bought this blender from you for $129 last week. BigMart sells it for $99. Will you match their price?" Your policy covers price adjustments when your own website's price drops within 14 days. It says nothing about matching competitors. The agent has a tool that can issue a price adjustment. What should the agent do?
questions.explanation: When policy is silent on a request, that's a policy gap. Escalate it rather than inventing a yes or a no.

choices.text: Approve the $30 adjustment, since price matching is common practice among retailers
choices.why: This makes policy on the fly and commits the company to something it never approved.

choices.text: Deny the request, because competitor price matching isn't listed in the policy
choices.why: The policy doesn't prohibit it either. A flat denial treats silence as a no.

choices.text: Escalate, because the policy says nothing about competitor matching
choices.why: Correct. A human with authority decides on a case the policy doesn't cover.

choices.text: Check the model's confidence, and approve the adjustment if it's above 80%
choices.why: Confidence doesn't fill a gap in policy, and self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated.

questions.prompt: A customer says, "I'm Maria Garcia, I want to return my order." The agent calls get_customer(name="Maria Garcia") and gets three matching accounts in different cities, each with recent orders. The customer hasn't given any other details yet. Returns involve refunding money to the account's payment method. What should the agent do?
questions.explanation: When a lookup returns several matches, ask for another identifier. Never guess, especially when money or account access is involved.

choices.text: Pick the most recently active account, since it's most likely to belong to the person chatting
choices.why: This is a guess, and it could refund money on the wrong person's account.

choices.text: Pick the account with an order that looks most like something someone would return
choices.why: This is another guess. A plausible-looking order doesn't confirm identity.

choices.text: Ask the customer for another identifier, such as email, order number or ZIP code
choices.why: Correct. One extra question resolves it with certainty.

choices.text: Show the customer all three accounts with their addresses, and ask which one is theirs
choices.why: This exposes two other customers' personal data.

questions.prompt: The support agent's first-contact resolution rate is 55%, against a target of 80%. Looking at the transcripts, it escalates simple cases (address changes, order-status questions) while trying to handle complex ones on its own (disputed charges, policy exceptions), sometimes badly. The system prompt says "Escalate when appropriate." What should you do first?
questions.explanation: Unclear escalation behaviour is fixed most directly with explicit criteria and few-shot examples showing when to escalate and when to resolve.

choices.text: Escalate whenever the model's self-reported confidence falls below 70%
choices.why: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated, and the agent is already confident on the wrong cases.

choices.text: Train a classifier on historical tickets to decide which conversations should be escalated
choices.why: This is a big investment before trying the cheap fix for the root cause, a vague instruction.

choices.text: Add explicit escalation criteria, with few-shot examples of escalating vs. resolving
choices.why: Correct. "Escalate disputed charges and policy exceptions; resolve address changes" removes the guesswork.

choices.text: Escalate based on customer sentiment, so that unhappy customers reach a person sooner
choices.why: Sentiment doesn't track case complexity. Calm customers can have complex disputes.

questions.prompt: The research coordinator sends five queries to the web search subagent. Four succeed. The fifth ("EU AI Act enforcement actions 2025") times out twice. The coordinator has to decide whether to retry, rephrase, try another source or note a gap in the report. Right now the subagent just returns {"status": "error"}. What should the subagent return to the coordinator?
questions.explanation: Error propagation should give the coordinator enough to decide: what failed, what was tried, any partial results, and possible alternatives.

choices.text: {"status": "error"}, plus the number of retries that were attempted
choices.why: The coordinator still doesn't know what kind of failure it was, or which query failed.

choices.text: An empty result set marked as success, so the other four results aren't held up
choices.why: This hides the failure, and the report may claim there were no enforcement actions.

choices.text: A structured error: failure type, the query, partial results and alternatives
choices.why: Correct. The coordinator can rephrase, reroute or report the gap with full context.

choices.text: Nothing, and the coordinator should stop the whole research workflow
choices.why: One timed-out query out of five doesn't justify losing all the work.

questions.prompt: Three hours into a Claude Code session exploring a large legacy codebase, Claude's answers turn generic. It describes "typical" service patterns that don't match the actual code, and forgets constraints you established in the first hour. Hundreds of Grep and Read results have built up in the context. You still have a lot of exploring to do. What helps most? (Select TWO.)
questions.explanation: Long exploration fills the context with stale tool output. Write findings to a durable scratchpad and summarize each phase, and move verbose investigation into subagents (compacting when needed).

choices.text: Write key findings to a scratchpad file, and summarize each phase before starting the next
choices.why: Correct. Findings are kept outside the context and can be reloaded as a concise summary.

choices.text: Delegate verbose investigation to subagents, and run /compact when discovery output fills the context
choices.why: Correct. Verbose output stays out of the main context, and compaction frees space.

choices.text: Keep going in the same session, since it will recover once you ask more specific questions
choices.why: Context pressure keeps growing. It won't recover by itself.

choices.text: Paste the whole repository into the prompt so Claude has every file available at once
choices.why: This makes the context-pressure problem much worse.

choices.text: Raise the temperature so that Claude's answers are less generic
choices.why: Randomness doesn't restore lost constraints or grounding.

questions.prompt: Your multi-agent research pipeline runs for 2 to 3 hours on large topics. Last week it crashed at hour two because of an infrastructure restart, and everything was rerun from scratch, including 40 minutes of paid web searches. All the state lived in the coordinator's context window. You want future crashes to cost minutes, not hours. How should you design for recovery?
questions.explanation: Design for resumption: each agent writes its state to a known location, and on restart the coordinator loads a manifest of what's done and continues from there.

choices.text: Rerun the whole pipeline from scratch after every crash, which is simpler and guarantees consistency
choices.why: This is the current approach, and it costs hours and repeated spend on every crash.

choices.text: Have each agent export its state to a known location, and load a manifest on resume
choices.why: Correct. Finished work is reloaded, and only unfinished tasks run again.

choices.text: Keep all state in the coordinator's context window, but use a model with a larger context
choices.why: Context is lost when the process crashes, whatever its size.

choices.text: Use --resume after a crash without saving any extra state from the subagents
choices.why: Resuming a session doesn't recover subagent work that was never saved.

questions.prompt: Your invoice extraction is 97% accurate overall on last month's 50,000 documents. Finance wants to drop human review entirely to save money. You haven't looked at accuracy by document type or by field, and you don't know whether the model's confidence scores track its actual errors. A wrong total_amount means a wrong payment. What should you do before reducing review?
questions.explanation: An aggregate figure can hide weak segments. Break accuracy down by document type and field, sample high-confidence outputs, and calibrate thresholds on labelled data before automating.

choices.text: Approve it, since 97% accuracy is high enough to remove human review safely
choices.why: The 3% could be concentrated in total_amount or in one vendor's invoices.

choices.text: Measure accuracy by type and field, and calibrate thresholds on a labelled set
choices.why: Correct. This shows where errors cluster and whether confidence can be trusted for routing.

choices.text: Ask the model to report its overall confidence in the pipeline and decide from that
choices.why: Self-assessment can't replace measurement against labelled data.

choices.text: Remove review now, and bring it back if complaints about incorrect payments start coming in
choices.why: Payment errors found through complaints are expensive and damage relationships.

questions.prompt: While researching a market report, the system finds two sources on the 2025 European heat-pump market. An industry association (published March 2025) puts it at €12.4B. An independent analyst firm (published January 2025) puts it at €9.8B. Neither explains its method in the excerpt. The report's readers will use the figure in investment decisions. What should the synthesis agent do?
questions.explanation: When sources conflict, report both with attribution and dates and flag the discrepancy. Don't silently choose, average or drop them.

choices.text: Report the larger figure, since the industry association is closer to the market
choices.why: Choosing one silently hides real uncertainty from readers making investment decisions.

choices.text: Average the two figures and report about €11.1B as the best estimate
choices.why: The average matches neither source and invents precision.

choices.text: Report both with source and publication date, and flag the discrepancy
choices.why: Correct. Readers see the range and the sources, and can judge for themselves.

choices.text: Leave both figures out, since sources that disagree can't be trusted
choices.why: Readers lose useful information, and the report hides that the question was examined.

questions.prompt: Your research system's final reports often attach citations to the wrong claims: a statistic credited to a news article that only quoted it, or a quote linked to the wrong paper. Subagents currently return prose summaries of their findings, and the report writer adds citations at the end. What fixes this at the source?
questions.explanation: Attribution has to be captured when a claim is found, not reconstructed later. Have subagents return structured claim-to-source mappings with an excerpt for each claim.

choices.text: Tell the report writer to add citations carefully and double-check each one
choices.why: The writer can only guess from prose that has already lost the link between claim and source.

choices.text: Have subagents return claim-to-source mappings (source, excerpt) with each finding
choices.why: Correct. Every claim arrives already attached to its evidence.

choices.text: Shorten the reports so there are fewer claims and fewer chances to mis-cite
choices.why: This reduces the problem without fixing it, and makes the reports less useful.

choices.text: Have the coordinator search afterwards for likely sources for each claim in the draft
choices.why: Reconstructing sources afterwards is how mis-attribution happens in the first place.

questions.prompt: In 2% of conversations the support agent calls process_refund before get_customer has confirmed the caller's identity. This usually happens when the customer opens with an order number and a demand. The system prompt already says "ALWAYS verify identity with get_customer before accessing orders or issuing refunds." Security has classed unverified refunds as a fraud risk. What is the most reliable fix?
questions.explanation: Ordering requirements with real stakes belong in code. A prerequisite gate blocks downstream tools until an earlier step has produced a verified result, so the order holds even when the model would have skipped it.

choices.text: A prerequisite gate that blocks process_refund and lookup_order until get_customer returns a verified ID
choices.why: Correct. The tools can't run out of order, whatever the customer says or how the model reasons.

choices.text: Move the verification instruction to the very top of the system prompt and repeat it again at the end
choices.why: Placement and repetition help a little. The rule is already stated plainly and still fails 2% of the time.

choices.text: Add few-shot examples showing verification before refunds, especially when the customer opens with an order number
choices.why: Better examples lower the rate, but a fraud risk needs a guarantee.

choices.text: Ask the model to state whether identity is verified before each tool call, and proceed only if it says yes
choices.why: The model judging its own compliance is the same judgement that is failing.

questions.prompt: A customer writes to the support agent: "Two things. I moved last week and need my shipping address updated on order #4471, which hasn't shipped yet. Also, my last invoice charged me twice for the same subscription." The two issues involve different records and tools. You want first-contact resolution and a clear answer for the customer. How should the agent handle this message?
questions.explanation: Separate concerns in one message should be decomposed and investigated independently, then answered together. Data from one investigation shouldn't leak into the other.

choices.text: Treat it as two concerns: investigate both, keep their data separate, and reply once
choices.why: Correct. Both issues get resolved in one contact without mixing records.

choices.text: Handle the address change, then ask the customer to start a new chat about the double charge
choices.why: This turns a first-contact resolution into two contacts for no good reason.

choices.text: Escalate to a human right away, since messages that raise more than one issue are too complex for the agent
choices.why: Two routine issues aren't a reason to escalate, and escalating hurts the resolution-rate goal.

choices.text: Combine both into one lookup_order call that pulls the order and billing records together
choices.why: lookup_order isn't a billing tool, and mixing the two lookups is how data gets confused.

questions.prompt: A user asks the research system about "the impact of AI on creative industries." The final report is well sourced and thorough, but covers only visual art. Music, writing and film are missing entirely. The trace shows the coordinator created three subtasks: "AI image generators", "AI in digital illustration" and "artist reactions to AI art". Each subagent did its task well, and synthesis faithfully combined what it received. What is the root cause?
questions.explanation: When every subagent did its job and the output is still incomplete, look at the decomposition. Coverage is fixed when the coordinator splits the work.

choices.text: The coordinator's decomposition of the topic was too narrow
choices.why: Correct. All three subtasks were about visual art, so no later stage could produce the rest.

choices.text: The web search subagent's queries were too short to surface sources about the other industries
choices.why: The search subagents were never asked about music, writing or film.

choices.text: The synthesis subagent dropped findings about the other industries when merging results
choices.why: The trace shows synthesis combined what it received faithfully. It received only visual art.

choices.text: The report subagent ran out of output tokens before it could write the remaining sections
choices.why: Running out of tokens would cut the report off mid-way. It wouldn't produce a complete report on one industry.

questions.prompt: The user asked the research system for a report covering six named subtopics. The synthesis subagent returns a strong draft that covers four of them. The other two (regulatory status and long-term cost) are missing because the search subagents found little on them in the first round. The report is due to the user in this same run. What should the coordinator do next?
questions.explanation: Coordinators should check output against the original request and loop back for targeted work on the gaps. Neither publishing an incomplete report nor filling gaps from model memory is acceptable.

choices.text: Re-delegate research on the two missing subtopics, then re-synthesize
choices.why: Correct. This is the iterative refinement loop: the gaps get targeted work and the rest is kept.

choices.text: Publish now, with a note at the top saying two requested subtopics may not be fully covered
choices.why: Being open about gaps is good, but the system hasn't tried to close them yet.

choices.text: Ask the synthesis subagent to write the two missing sections from its own general knowledge
choices.why: This produces uncited content in a cited report, which is worse than a visible gap.

choices.text: Restart the whole pipeline with the same plan and hope the second run covers everything
choices.why: This repeats the same decomposition and throws away the four good sections.

questions.prompt: In the research system, the web-search subagent finds a 120-page PDF that looks central to the question. The document-analysis subagent is the right one to read it. A developer suggests giving the search subagent the Task tool so it can call the analysis subagent directly with the link, "to save a round trip through the coordinator." How should the PDF reach the analysis subagent?
questions.explanation: In a hub-and-spoke design, subagents report to the coordinator and the coordinator decides what to delegate. This keeps routing, observability and error handling in one place.

choices.text: Back through the coordinator, which decides whether to delegate it to the analysis subagent
choices.why: Correct. The coordinator keeps the full picture and can weigh this PDF against everything else.

choices.text: The search subagent calls the analysis subagent directly with the PDF link, as the developer suggests
choices.why: Peer-to-peer calls hide work from the coordinator and make failures harder to trace.

choices.text: Both subagents read and write a shared conversation history so each sees what the other found
choices.why: Shared history defeats the isolated, focused context that makes subagents useful.

choices.text: The analysis subagent polls the search subagent's output folder on a timer for newly found documents
choices.why: Polling adds latency and coupling, and nobody owns the decision about what gets analyzed.

questions.prompt: The research coordinator has gathered 23 findings from four subagents, each with a source URL, publication date and page number. It now has to hand them to the synthesis subagent, which must write a report with accurate inline citations. Past reports mixed up which claim came from which source. Which way of passing the findings works best?
questions.explanation: Pass findings in the subagent's prompt in a structured form that keeps each claim attached to its source metadata. That is what makes accurate attribution possible.

choices.text: In the prompt, as structured findings with content kept apart from source metadata
choices.why: Correct. Each claim travels with its URL, date and page, so citations can't come loose.

choices.text: As a one-line summary of the overall conclusions, to keep the synthesis prompt short
choices.why: This saves tokens but loses the per-claim sources the report needs.

choices.text: By telling the subagent to look back at the coordinator's conversation for the details
choices.why: Subagents can't see the coordinator's conversation.

choices.text: As the full raw text of every fetched page, concatenated in the order the pages were retrieved
choices.why: Everything is technically there, but claims and sources are buried and easy to mismatch.

questions.prompt: You are defining the research system's document-analysis subagent with an AgentDefinition. It will read PDFs and web pages the coordinator passes to it and return structured findings. It should never browse the web itself or write files. You want the coordinator to delegate to it at the right times, and you want it limited to what it needs. Which belong in the AgentDefinition? (Select TWO.)
questions.explanation: An AgentDefinition says what the subagent is for (so the coordinator knows when to use it) and which tools it may use. Context is passed per task in the prompt. It isn't baked into the definition.

choices.text: A description of what the subagent is for
choices.why: Correct. The coordinator uses the description to decide when to delegate.

choices.text: Tool restrictions limiting it to the tools it needs
choices.why: Correct. Least privilege keeps it focused and stops it browsing or writing files.

choices.text: A copy of the coordinator's full conversation history, so the subagent has all the background
choices.why: Definitions are static, and history is the wrong thing to pass. Give it task context in the prompt.

choices.text: A list of the other subagents it may call directly when it needs help with a document
choices.why: Subagents report to the coordinator. They don't call each other.

choices.text: The coordinator's allowedTools list, including "Task", so it has the same capabilities
choices.why: This gives the subagent more than it needs, including the ability to spawn agents.

questions.prompt: lookup_order returns status as numeric codes: 1 = processing, 2 = shipped, 3 = delivered, 7 = cancelled. A table explaining the codes was added to the system prompt last month. Since then, about 1 in 200 conversations still tells a customer that a cancelled order has shipped, and that has led to chargebacks. The tool belongs to another team and won't change soon. What is the most reliable fix?
questions.explanation: Translate machine codes into readable values in a PostToolUse hook, so the model never has to interpret them. Deterministic transforms beat prompt-level lookup tables.

choices.text: A PostToolUse hook that maps each status code to a readable status before the model sees it
choices.why: Correct. The model reads "cancelled", not "7", so there is nothing to misinterpret.

choices.text: Expand the system prompt table with examples of each code in context and a warning about code 7
choices.why: This is the approach already in place. More detail may help, but interpretation stays probabilistic.

choices.text: Have the agent call lookup_order twice for every order and compare the two results before replying
choices.why: Both calls return the same code. The misreading happens after the tool returns.

choices.text: An interception hook that blocks lookup_order until a human confirms what the returned code means
choices.why: This puts a human in every order lookup and wrecks the resolution-time goal.

questions.prompt: For refunds, the steps are always the same: verify identity, look up the order, check it against the refund policy, then either refund or escalate. Leadership wants that order guaranteed for audit purposes, because skipping the policy check has caused overpayments. The agent should still handle the conversation around these steps naturally. Which design fits?
questions.explanation: When the sequence is known and must hold, enforce it in code with prerequisites between the steps, and let the model handle the conversation around them.

choices.text: Enforce the sequence in code, with prerequisites between the steps
choices.why: Correct. Each step is gated on the previous one, so the order can be audited and guaranteed.

choices.text: Let the model choose the order, and log every deviation from the expected order for a weekly review
choices.why: This finds overpayments after they happen. It doesn't prevent them.

choices.text: State the required order in bold capitals in the system prompt, and repeat it before every tool result
choices.why: Still a prompt-level rule. Emphasis improves compliance but can't guarantee it.

choices.text: Give the model all four tools at once with tool_choice "auto" so it can work out the best order itself
choices.why: This leaves the order entirely to the model, which is what leadership wants to avoid.

questions.prompt: You use an Agent SDK workflow to review pull requests. A 40-file PR passes review in a single pass, but after merging, an interface change in api/client.ts breaks callers in three other files that were also in the PR. Re-reading the transcript, the reviewer commented in detail on each file but never connected the signature change to its callers. What is the better approach?
questions.explanation: Large reviews benefit from multiple passes: focused per-file passes for local issues, plus a separate integration pass that looks at how the changes interact across files.

choices.text: Per-file review passes plus a separate cross-file integration pass
choices.why: Correct. Local depth comes from the per-file passes, and the integration pass catches problems like the broken callers.

choices.text: A single pass with a longer prompt that asks the reviewer to pay special attention to interface changes
choices.why: One pass over 40 files spreads attention thin, and that was the original failure.

choices.text: Review only the files with the most changed lines, since they are where most bugs come from
choices.why: The breaking change could be a one-line signature edit. Line count says little about risk.

choices.text: Forty fully independent reviews, one per file, with no combined step afterwards
choices.why: Each file gets attention, but nothing looks across files, so the same bug gets through.

questions.prompt: Your CI pipeline runs Claude on every pull request. Each PR needs the same three checks, every time: a security review, a test coverage assessment and a documentation check. Each produces a separate section in the PR comment. The checks never change from PR to PR, and you want consistent, auditable output. Which decomposition fits this work?
questions.explanation: When the steps are known and stable, a fixed prompt chain is simpler, cheaper and more predictable than dynamic decomposition. Save adaptive planning for open-ended work.

choices.text: Fixed prompt chaining, with one step per check
choices.why: Correct. Each step is focused, and the output is consistent from PR to PR.

choices.text: Dynamic decomposition, letting the model plan a fresh set of review steps for each pull request
choices.why: Adaptive planning adds variance and cost to a process that never changes.

choices.text: A single prompt that asks for the security, coverage and documentation checks all at once
choices.why: Combining unrelated checks dilutes attention, and each section comes out shallower.

choices.text: A coordinator that delegates to a dozen general-purpose subagents and merges what they return
choices.why: This is a lot of orchestration for three fixed checks.

questions.prompt: You plan to resume yesterday's Claude Code analysis session on an order-processing service. Overnight, a large refactor merged that renamed most modules, moved files between packages and split two classes. Your conclusions about the business rules still hold, but nearly every file path and tool result in the session is now out of date. What is the best move?
questions.explanation: When most of a session's tool results are stale, resuming does more harm than good. Start fresh and inject a short summary of the conclusions that still hold.

choices.text: Start fresh and inject a short summary of the conclusions that still hold
choices.why: Correct. You keep the insights and drop the misleading file paths and tool results.

choices.text: Resume the session and rely on the earlier tool results, since the business logic is unchanged
choices.why: The model would act on paths and structures that no longer exist.

choices.text: Resume the session, paste in the list of renamed modules, and ask it to re-check each one
choices.why: Telling it which files changed works when a few changed. Here almost everything did, and the stale context still competes.

choices.text: Fork yesterday's session and continue the analysis on the new branch
choices.why: A fork inherits the same stale context.

questions.prompt: A developer writes their own agentic loop on the Messages API. After each tool call, the loop sends a new request containing only the system prompt and the latest tool result. In testing, the agent repeats tool calls it has already made, forgets what the user asked, and sometimes answers a different question. What is the fix?
questions.explanation: The Messages API is stateless. Each request must include the full conversation: the user's turns, the assistant's tool_use blocks and the matching tool_result blocks.

choices.text: Append each tool result to the history and send the full history on the next request
choices.why: Correct. The model sees what was asked, what it has already done and what came back.

choices.text: Keep sending only the latest tool result, but make each result more detailed and self-contained
choices.why: A richer tool result still leaves out the user's question and the earlier steps.

choices.text: Move every tool result into the system prompt so the model sees all of them on each request
choices.why: This misuses the system prompt and breaks the tool_use/tool_result pairing the API expects.

choices.text: Start a new conversation for each tool call, carrying over only the user's first message
choices.why: This throws away every previous tool result, which is the same problem in another form.

questions.prompt: You are reviewing three teams' Agent SDK loops before launch. The teams use different rules to decide when the loop is finished. Some of those rules have caused agents to stop with work unfinished, or to stop right after announcing a tool call they never made. Which are anti-patterns for deciding that an agentic loop is finished? (Select TWO.)
questions.explanation: Loop termination should rest on stop_reason. Text in the response isn't a completion signal, because a response can contain text and a tool request together.

choices.text: Treating any assistant text in the response as the completion signal
choices.why: Correct, it's an anti-pattern. Text often comes alongside a tool_use block.

choices.text: Looking for phrases like "I'm done" in the model's reply
choices.why: Correct, it's an anti-pattern. Phrase matching is brittle and can't see a pending tool call.

choices.text: Stopping when stop_reason is "end_turn"
choices.why: This is the right stop condition.

choices.text: Continuing while stop_reason is "tool_use"
choices.why: This is the right continue condition.

choices.text: Keeping an iteration cap as a safety net
choices.why: A cap as a backstop against runaway loops is fine, as long as it isn't the main stop condition.

questions.prompt: For a comparative question, the research coordinator needs three independent web searches (EU policy, US policy and China policy) and then one synthesis step that compares all three. The current trace runs all four steps one after another. A teammate suggests firing all four Task calls at once to minimise latency. How should the coordinator issue the work?
questions.explanation: Parallelize independent work, and sequence dependent work. Synthesis depends on all three searches, so it can only start once they have returned.

choices.text: Emit the three search Task calls in one response, then synthesis once they return
choices.why: Correct. The searches run in parallel, and synthesis runs once, with every input available.

choices.text: Emit all four Task calls in one response, including the synthesis step
choices.why: Synthesis would start with no search results to compare.

choices.text: Run all four Task calls one after another, as the current trace does
choices.why: This works, but wastes the time the three independent searches could save.

choices.text: Ask a single subagent to run all three searches itself and then write the synthesis
choices.why: This serializes the work inside one context and loses the parallelism.

questions.prompt: An interception hook on process_refund blocks a $900 refund because it exceeds the $500 automatic limit. The customer has been waiting and is frustrated. The hook returns a block result to the agent. Product wants the customer's issue handled without breaking policy, and support wants the case in the human queue with full context. What should happen next?
questions.explanation: A blocked action should go to the right human path with full context. The agent must never work around the control or pretend the action succeeded.

choices.text: Escalate the case to a human with the customer, order and amount
choices.why: Correct. The policy holds and the customer is still helped, by someone who has the context.

choices.text: Drop the call quietly and have the agent tell the customer the refund has been processed
choices.why: This lies to the customer and buries a policy event.

choices.text: Let the agent split the refund into two payments of $450 so that each stays under the limit
choices.why: This is deliberately working around a financial control.

choices.text: Lower the refund to $500 automatically, process it, and leave the remaining $400 for later
choices.why: This changes the outcome without approval and leaves the case half-handled.

questions.prompt: Your developer-productivity agent has one tool, analyze_document(path, instructions), used for three different jobs: summarizing design docs, extracting tables from specs, and checking documents against a compliance checklist. Its description says "Analyzes a document." The agent often asks for a summary when a table was needed, or runs the compliance check without the checklist. What should you do?
questions.explanation: A tool that does several unrelated jobs pushes the hard choice into free-text instructions. Purpose-specific tools with clear descriptions and parameters make each job explicit.

choices.text: Split it into purpose-specific tools, such as summarize_document and extract_tables
choices.why: Correct. Each tool has a clear description and the right parameters, such as a required checklist for compliance.

choices.text: Add a mode parameter to analyze_document, and keep its current one-line description
choices.why: Without a better description the model still can't tell when each mode applies.

choices.text: Add a line to the system prompt telling the model to be careful whenever it calls analyze_document
choices.why: A vague caution doesn't tell the model how to choose.

choices.text: Remove the tool and let the agent read every document with the built-in Read tool, then analyze it inline
choices.why: You lose the structure and the reliable table extraction the tool provides.

questions.prompt: After you rewrote the support agent's tool descriptions, lookup_order and get_customer are detailed and clearly distinct. Even so, the agent now calls lookup_order on almost every message, including "hi" and "what's your return policy?" The system prompt, written by the product team, contains the line: "ORDER LOOKUP IS CRITICAL. ALWAYS LOOK UP ORDERS." What should you check first?
questions.explanation: Strong, keyword-heavy wording in the system prompt can override good tool descriptions. When tool choice is skewed toward one tool, check the system prompt before changing the tools.

choices.text: Whether the keyword-heavy system prompt is overriding the tool descriptions
choices.why: Correct. The shouted line is the likeliest reason the agent calls lookup_order on everything.

choices.text: Whether lookup_order needs an even longer description with more example queries and edge cases
choices.why: The descriptions are already good, and this would make lookup_order even more attractive.

choices.text: Whether the agent needs more tools to choose from, so that lookup_order stops being its default
choices.why: More tools wouldn't remove the instruction that is skewing the choice.

choices.text: Whether tool_choice should force get_customer on every turn so lookup_order is called less often
choices.why: Forcing a different tool every turn creates its own wrong calls, on greetings and policy questions alike.

questions.prompt: Midway through a research job, the web search subagent gets an HTTP 429 rate-limit error from the search API on its fourth query. Three earlier queries succeeded and returned useful results. The rate limit usually clears within a few seconds. The coordinator is waiting on this subagent along with three others. What should happen?
questions.explanation: Handle transient errors close to where they happen: retry locally with backoff. If the subagent still fails, escalate to the coordinator with what it tried and the partial results it has.

choices.text: Retry locally, and if it still fails, escalate with what it tried and the partial results
choices.why: Correct. A brief blip is absorbed, and a lasting failure reaches the coordinator with useful context.

choices.text: Return an empty result list marked as success, so that the coordinator isn't held up
choices.why: Hiding a failure as success leads the coordinator to conclude there are no sources.

choices.text: Have the coordinator abort the whole research job as soon as the error is reported
choices.why: One transient error on one query isn't a reason to throw away all the other work.

choices.text: Return "Operation failed" to the coordinator and stop all work on that query, discarding the three good results
choices.why: This throws away good results and gives the coordinator nothing to act on.

questions.prompt: A customer asks for a refund on an order delivered 41 days ago. Store policy allows refunds within 30 days. process_refund correctly rejects the request. You are designing its error response so the agent handles this well: it should explain the policy to the customer, not retry, and offer alternatives such as store credit where the policy allows it. How should the MCP tool report this?
questions.explanation: A policy rejection is a business error. It isn't retryable, and it needs a readable reason the agent can pass on. Labelling it as transient would cause pointless retries.

choices.text: isError: true, errorCategory "business", isRetryable: false, and a readable reason
choices.why: Correct. The agent knows not to retry and can explain the 30-day policy.

choices.text: isError: true, errorCategory "transient", isRetryable: true
choices.why: Retrying a policy decision always gives the same answer, and the agent wastes calls.

choices.text: A success response with an empty body, which the agent can read as "nothing to refund"
choices.why: The agent may tell the customer the refund went through.

choices.text: A generic "Operation failed" message, which keeps internal refund-policy details out of the response
choices.why: The agent can't explain the outcome or decide what to offer instead.

questions.prompt: You are writing an error-response standard for every MCP tool the support agent uses. Today, errors are free-text strings, and the agent sometimes retries a declined card ten times, or gives up on a timeout that would have succeeded a second later. The standard should let the agent decide what to do next without guessing. Which fields make a tool error actionable for the agent? (Select TWO.)
questions.explanation: An actionable error says what kind of failure happened and whether retrying could help. Those two facts drive the agent's next move.

choices.text: errorCategory, such as transient, validation, business or permission
choices.why: Correct. The category tells the agent how to respond.

choices.text: isRetryable, saying whether trying again could succeed
choices.why: Correct. This stops pointless retries and allows useful ones.

choices.text: The server's full stack trace, so the agent can work out the cause of the failure itself
choices.why: This is noise for the agent and may leak internal details.

choices.text: The version of the HTTP library the server uses, for debugging
choices.why: This doesn't help the agent decide anything.

choices.text: A random retry delay for the model to wait before calling the tool again
choices.why: Backoff belongs in client code, not in a wait the model is asked to perform.

questions.prompt: The research system's synthesis subagent has a generic fetch_url tool. It's meant for re-reading documents the search subagent has already vetted, but transcripts show it sometimes fetches unvetted pages, such as forums or SEO spam, and cites them in the final report. The research team requires every cited source to be one the search stage approved. What is the better tool design?
questions.explanation: Constrain what a tool can do to what the role needs. A tool that can only load vetted documents enforces the rule. Asking the model to be careful doesn't.

choices.text: Replace fetch_url with a constrained load_document tool
choices.why: Correct. If it can only load approved document IDs, unvetted pages can't get into the report.

choices.text: Keep fetch_url, and add a line to its description asking the subagent to stick to vetted sources
choices.why: This is a soft instruction for a hard requirement, and it will fail sometimes.

choices.text: Give the synthesis subagent all the web search tools too, so it can vet new sources itself
choices.why: This widens its reach and blurs the split between search and synthesis.

choices.text: Let the synthesis subagent call the web search subagent directly whenever it wants another page
choices.why: This bypasses the coordinator and still lets unvetted material in.

questions.prompt: While writing reports, the synthesis subagent often needs to check a single fact, such as a date or a statistic. Today each check goes from synthesis to the coordinator, then to the web search subagent and back, which adds about 30 seconds per fact. Most reports need 5 to 10 checks. You want faster reports without giving up the separation between broad research and synthesis. What is the recommended change?
questions.explanation: Give a subagent narrowly scoped tools for frequent small needs, and leave broad capabilities with the specialist agent. This cuts round trips while keeping roles clear.

choices.text: Give synthesis a scoped verify_fact tool, and leave broad searching to the search subagent
choices.why: Correct. Quick checks happen locally, and open-ended research stays where it belongs.

choices.text: Give the synthesis subagent every web search tool, so it never has to wait on the coordinator
choices.why: This removes the separation of roles and invites synthesis to do unvetted research.

choices.text: Let the synthesis subagent message the search subagent directly for each fact it checks
choices.why: Peer-to-peer messaging bypasses the coordinator's routing and visibility.

choices.text: Skip fact verification during synthesis and rely on the search stage having been accurate
choices.why: This trades accuracy for speed in a system whose job is accurate reports.

questions.prompt: A developer on your team wants to try an experimental MCP server that connects Claude Code to their personal note-taking app. It's unstable, needs their own API key, and nobody else on the team needs it. The project already has a committed .mcp.json with the team's shared servers. Where should the experimental server be configured?
questions.explanation: User-scoped configuration in ~/.claude.json is for servers only one person needs. Project scope (.mcp.json) is for servers the whole team shares.

choices.text: In their user-level ~/.claude.json
choices.why: Correct. It's available only to them, across their projects, and doesn't affect anyone else.

choices.text: In the project's .mcp.json, committed to the repo so it's easy to find and remove later
choices.why: This would push an unstable personal server onto every teammate.

choices.text: In the project's CLAUDE.md, under a section for experimental tools
choices.why: CLAUDE.md is for instructions. It doesn't configure MCP servers.

choices.text: In .claude/commands/, as a slash command that starts the server when they need it
choices.why: Slash commands are prompt templates. They don't register MCP servers.

questions.prompt: Your project's .mcp.json configures two servers: a GitHub server (issues, PRs, code search) and a Jira server (tickets, sprints). A teammate asks whether Claude Code will use only the first one listed, or whether they need to switch between them, because they want an agent that links each PR to its Jira ticket in one task. How does the agent get the tools from these servers?
questions.explanation: Tools from all configured MCP servers are available together, alongside the built-in tools, so one task can combine them.

choices.text: Tools from both servers are available at the same time
choices.why: Correct. The agent can read a PR and update its Jira ticket in the same task.

choices.text: Only the first server listed in .mcp.json is active, and the others are kept as fallbacks
choices.why: All configured servers are connected. List order doesn't make one primary.

choices.text: You choose one server per session, and switch servers with a command when you need the other
choices.why: There's no switching. Both are available together.

choices.text: Their tools replace the built-in tools such as Read and Grep while either server is connected
choices.why: MCP tools are added alongside the built-in tools. They don't replace them.

questions.prompt: You joined a team last week and are asked to change how refunds are calculated. You need to understand how the functions exported from payments/api.ts are used across a 3,000-file codebase you've never seen, including indirect use through re-exports. You're using Claude Code's built-in tools. Which approach fits?
questions.explanation: Explore a large unfamiliar codebase incrementally: Grep to find entry points and references, Read to follow imports, then trace names through re-exports. Don't read everything up front.

choices.text: Grep for entry points, Read to follow imports, then trace the exported names
choices.why: Correct. This is targeted, and it follows real usage, including re-exports.

choices.text: Read every file in the repository in alphabetical order to build a complete picture first
choices.why: This floods the context with irrelevant code and still doesn't show how the pieces connect.

choices.text: Glob for every *.ts file, then Write a short summary of each one before looking for callers
choices.why: This produces thousands of summaries before you even start on the question.
