choices.text: Use Edit to add logging to every file that might call it, then run the app and read the logs
choices.why: This changes code just to explore it, and only shows the paths you happen to exercise.

questions.prompt: The support agent handles a mix of messages. Some need a tool ("where is order #8812?"), and others should get a plain text answer ("what is your return policy?" or "thanks, that's all"). In testing with tool_choice set to "any", the agent called lookup_order on policy questions and on thank-you messages. Which tool_choice setting fits this agent?
questions.explanation: "auto" lets the model decide whether to call a tool or answer in text. "any" forces some tool call, and a named tool forces that tool. Use the forcing settings only when a call must happen.

choices.text: "auto"
choices.why: Correct. The agent calls tools when it needs data and answers in text otherwise.

choices.text: "any"
choices.why: This forces a tool call on every turn, which caused the problem in testing.

choices.text: {"type": "tool", "name": "lookup_order"}
choices.why: This forces lookup_order every time, which is worse than "any".

choices.text: Remove all tools from the request
choices.why: The agent could then never look up an order.

questions.prompt: Your project's root CLAUDE.md has grown to 900 lines over a year. It covers testing, API style, database migrations, deployment, the frontend design system and incident runbooks. Different teams edit different sections, merge conflicts in the file are common, and nobody is sure which parts are still current. What is the most maintainable structure?
questions.explanation: Split a large memory file by topic: either .claude/rules/ files (path-scoped where that makes sense) or separate files pulled in with @import. Each topic gets its own owner and history.

choices.text: Split topics into files under .claude/rules/, or pull them in with @import
choices.why: Correct. Each topic is a separate file with clearer ownership and fewer conflicts, and path-scoped rules can load only when relevant.

choices.text: Keep one file, but add a table of contents and clear headings so Claude can find each topic
choices.why: This makes it easier to read, but conflicts, ownership and size don't change.

choices.text: Move everything to ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, where file length matters less than in the project file
choices.why: That makes it personal and unshared, so teammates lose it.

choices.text: Move it into a commands array in .claude/config.json so each section loads only when needed
choices.why: That mechanism doesn't exist.

questions.prompt: You wrote your team's REST API conventions (resource naming, error envelope, pagination) into ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. Claude follows them perfectly in your sessions. A teammate working in the same repo says Claude ignores them completely. They're on the same Claude Code version and branch, and they ran /memory, which doesn't list your conventions. Why?
questions.explanation: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is user-level and exists only on your machine. Team conventions belong in the project's CLAUDE.md (or .claude/rules/), committed to the repo.

choices.text: The user-level file isn't shared. Move the conventions to the project's CLAUDE.md
choices.why: Correct. Once it's committed, everyone who pulls gets the conventions.

choices.text: Your teammate needs to run /compact to reload the memory files in their session
choices.why: /compact summarizes the conversation. It can't load a file that only exists on your machine.

choices.text: CLAUDE.md files are only loaded in plan mode, and your teammate is using direct execution
choices.why: CLAUDE.md loads in every mode.

choices.text: Conventions have to be defined in .mcp.json to be shared across the team
choices.why: .mcp.json configures MCP servers, not instructions.

questions.prompt: A teammate opens a PR that adds a "commands" array to .claude/config.json, defining a shared /release command with a name, description and prompt. They say it's "cleaner than lots of little Markdown files." Nothing in Claude Code's documentation mentions this format, and the command doesn't appear when they type /. What should you tell them?
questions.explanation: Project commands are Markdown files in .claude/commands/. A "commands" array in config.json isn't a Claude Code mechanism.

choices.text: That format doesn't exist. Add .claude/commands/release.md to the repo instead
choices.why: Correct. The file name becomes the command name, and the file's contents are the prompt.

choices.text: It's a good idea, and it will work as long as .claude/config.json is committed
choices.why: Committing the file doesn't make an unsupported format work.

choices.text: Define the /release command inside the project's CLAUDE.md instead of config.json
choices.why: CLAUDE.md doesn't define slash commands.

choices.text: Put it in ~/.claude.json instead, which everyone who clones the repository shares
choices.why: ~/.claude.json is a per-user file. It isn't part of the repo.

questions.prompt: Your team has a 400-line database-migration checklist: backup verification, lock-timeout settings, backfill strategy and rollback steps. It's needed a few times a month. When it lived in the root CLAUDE.md, it cost tokens in every session and seemed to dilute attention to the other instructions. Where should it live?
questions.explanation: Skills load only when invoked or when they're relevant, which suits detailed procedures needed occasionally. CLAUDE.md is for guidance that applies in every session.

choices.text: In a skill under .claude/skills/, which loads only when needed
choices.why: Correct. It's shared with the team and stays out of context until a migration comes up.

choices.text: In the root CLAUDE.md, so it's always available whenever someone does a migration
choices.why: This is what caused the cost and dilution problem in the first place.

choices.text: In ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, which Claude only reads when you ask about databases
choices.why: User-level CLAUDE.md loads in every session, and it isn't shared.

choices.text: In the project's .mcp.json, next to the database server's configuration
choices.why: .mcp.json configures servers. It can't hold a checklist.

questions.prompt: Your team's /scaffold-service skill generates a new microservice. It needs a service name, which it uses for directories, package names and Kubernetes manifests. People often run it without one. Claude then invents a name like "new-service", and someone has to rename files by hand. You want the expected argument to be obvious when the skill is invoked. Which SKILL.md frontmatter key helps?
questions.explanation: argument-hint shows users what arguments a skill expects when they invoke it, which reduces calls with missing arguments.

choices.text: argument-hint
choices.why: Correct. A hint such as <service-name> appears when the skill is invoked.

choices.text: context: fork

questions.prompt: A customer wants help with an order. They've given an order number (not found), the email they think they used (no account), and a phone number (an account with no orders). questions.prompt: Your extraction model outputs a confidence score per field, from 0 to 1. You plan to auto-accept fields above a threshold and send the rest to human review. A teammate suggests using 0.9 for every field, "since that's high enough to be safe." You have 2,000 documents with human-verified labels. How should you choose the threshold?
questions.explanation: Choose confidence thresholds empirically. Calibrate them against labelled data (per field where it matters), instead of trusting raw scores or round numbers.

choices.text: Calibrate it against a labelled validation set
choices.why: Correct. You find which score actually gives acceptable accuracy, field by field.

questions.prompt: Your human review team can check only about 5% of the 20,000 extractions processed each week. Today they review whatever arrived most recently. You want their time to catch as many errors as possible, and also to show whether high-confidence extractions are really as accurate as their scores suggest. Where should their time go? (Select TWO.)
questions.explanation: Send uncertain or contradictory items to review (where the errors are most likely), and spot-check high-confidence items with stratified random sampling (to verify calibration).

choices.text: Low-confidence or contradictory extractions
choices.why: Correct. This is where errors are most likely, so review time pays off most.

choices.text: A stratified random sample of high-confidence extractions
choices.why: Correct. It checks that auto-accepted items deserve their confidence, across document types.

choices.why: These are least likely to contain errors, so reviewing only them wastes most of the time.
